results.title: Ransomware Recovery: What Happens in the First 24 Hours
results.author: Chris Turn
results.content:
A ransomware attack rarely announces itself with fanfare. One moment, your systems are humming along; the next, files are encrypted, screens display ransom notes, and panic sets in. How your organization responds in the first 24 hours can determine whether this becomes a manageable disruption or a catastrophic loss. Cybersecurity experts agree: the actions taken immediately after discovery matter more than almost anything else in the recovery process.
Hour One: Containment Is Everything
The instant ransomware is detected, the priority shifts to containment. This means isolating infected devices from the network immediately—disconnecting from Wi-Fi, unplugging ethernet cables, and disabling shared drives. The goal is to stop the malware from spreading laterally to other systems, servers, or backup locations.
During this phase, resist the urge to power down infected machines completely. Forensic investigators often need the system in its current state to understand how the attack unfolded. Instead, isolate and preserve. This distinction can make a significant difference when it comes time to investigate root causes and strengthen defenses against future incidents.
Hours Two to Four: Assemble the Response Team
Once containment is underway, it’s time to activate your incident response plan. This typically involves IT and cybersecurity staff, but it should also include legal counsel, communications or PR personnel, and executive leadership. Ransomware isn’t just a technical problem; it’s a business crisis with legal, financial, and reputational implications.
If your organization doesn’t have in-house cybersecurity expertise, this is the moment to bring in outside specialists. Many businesses maintain relationships with incident response firms specifically so they can mobilize quickly rather than scrambling to find help mid-crisis. Time lost searching for assistance is time the attackers use to their advantage.
Hours Four to Twelve: Assess the Damage
With containment measures in place and the right people involved, the focus turns to assessment. What systems were affected? What data was encrypted or potentially exfiltrated? Is there evidence the attackers accessed sensitive customer or employee information?
This is also when many organizations determine whether clean, uninfected backups exist. A well-maintained backup strategy—with copies stored offline or in immutable cloud storage—can be the difference between a quick recovery and a prolonged, costly ordeal. If backups are compromised or unavailable, the path forward becomes considerably more complicated.
Hours Twelve to Eighteen: Notification and Communication
Depending on your industry and jurisdiction, you may be legally required to notify regulators, customers, or partners about the breach within a specific timeframe. Legal counsel should guide this process carefully, as premature or inaccurate communications can create additional liability.
Internally, transparent communication with employees is equally important. Staff need clear instructions about what systems are safe to use, what information they should avoid sharing, and who to contact with questions. Confusion and misinformation can compound an already stressful situation.
Hours Eighteen to Twenty-Four: Decision Point
By the latter part of the first day, most organizations face a critical decision: restore from backups, rebuild systems from scratch, or—controversially—consider paying the ransom. Cybersecurity professionals generally advise against paying, as it doesn’t guarantee data recovery and may encourage further attacks. Still, every situation is different, and this decision often involves input from legal counsel, law enforcement, and executive leadership.
Beyond the First Day
The first 24 hours are just the beginning. Full recovery often takes weeks, involving system rebuilds, security audits, and policy updates to prevent recurrence. Organizations that weather ransomware attacks most successfully are typically those that prepared in advance: regular backups, employee training, and a documented response plan tested before disaster strikes.
Ransomware attacks are a growing reality for businesses of every size. While no organization can eliminate risk entirely, having a clear, well-rehearsed plan for those crucial first hours can mean the difference between a swift recovery and a prolonged crisis.
SME Paid Under
results.summary:
Organizations can mitigate the impact of a ransomware attack by following a structured 24-hour response plan focused on immediate system containment, expert coordination, and strategic damage assessment.

### Key Points
- Isolate infected devices from networks immediately by disconnecting Wi-Fi and ethernet cables to prevent the malware from spreading laterally.
- Preserve system states rather than powering down machines to ensure forensic investigators can identify the root cause of the breach.
- Activate an incident response team within four hours, including IT staff, legal counsel, communications experts, and executive leadership.
- Verify the integrity of offline or immutable cloud backups to determine if data restoration is possible without paying a ransom.
- Consult with legal counsel regarding mandatory notification requirements for regulators, customers, and partners to manage potential liability.

### Why it Matters
A rapid and organized response during the first day of a cyberattack significantly reduces the risk of catastrophic data loss and long-term operational disruption. Organizations that prioritize preparation and clear communication are better positioned to navigate the legal, financial, and reputational challenges inherent in ransomware incidents.

results.title: The Rise and Fall of Jev
results.author: Alex Ewerlöf
results.content:
This is a quick note on how the industry’s reaction to Jev reveals the desperate state of AI. I’ll dissect:
- What is Jev, how was it hyped and why it spread like mass hysteria? Jev isn’t dead but its hype cycle is. Decision models are on the rise.
- What are the noteworthy innovations since ChatGPT brought “AI” to the mainstream?
- Why is the industry starved from real innovation and what high impact problems are still unsolved after 4 years of revolution incremental improvements?
The point is to use Jev’s hype cycle to call out the manipulative marketing that are too familiar with at this point.
Jev
You probably don’t need an intro to Jev at this time because since its introduction 33 days ago, it has been all the rage!
But if you were clever enough to ignore it, here’s what actually matters:
Jev is basically a general purpose classifier (e.g. quick judgement). What makes it interesting is that you don’t have to train it with a lot of data (although that lack of special-purpose training negatively impacts its utility).
Calling it a “decision model” is a bit far fetched especially since it cannot even see (rival open-weight models have multi-modal features) or reason (that’s how it’s so cheap).
The idea behind Jev isn’t new! The idea of non-autoregressive decision models with RL goes back more than a year ago. The original author is pissed but as we’ll see drama is an inseparable part of AI hype.
Hype
I want to walk you through the emotional roller-coaster I went through when I read their announcement via hackernews:
At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT.
😎 So the founder was behind ChatGPT, one of the fastest-growing products in history. I’m listening…
At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing.
😃 Oh, my god! This is it! ChatGPT is missing something big and he’s about to reveal it! We’re one step closer to AGI if we haven’t reached it already! I’m thrilled to read more…
After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce
😱 Spit it out! I’m beyond excited to read this…
TypeSafe AI is releasing our first System One Model
😯 Wait what?!! “System one”?
Do you understand what you’re talking about? Here’s my recollection of how Daniel Kahneman defined the two systems:
- System one: fast, cheap (in terms of computational power), emotional, unconscious and judgmental.
- System two: slow, expensive (takes more brain power), logical, conscious, and more elaborate.
If Jev is system one then LM is system two? It can’t even handle logical reasoning!
Most importantly Jev came with another interesting framing:
can’t hallucinate
Hallucination is one of the biggest problems with the current generation of language models but no hallucination doesn’t mean the response is logically correct. In Jev’s context, it just means that the output matches the schema.
Technically conventional language models can gain this ability by bolting a control loop (e.g., type checker, JSON schema parser) on top. Jev does this much faster and without reasoning. It’s in the name:
We named Jev after William Stanley Jevons. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar path to coal, after steam-engine efficiency led to an increase in demand.
I don’t know Jev’s architecture because in the true ex-"Open”AI employee tradition, not much is released (probably in the name of “safety” or “moat”). But that doesn’t stop them from dropping jargons:
We built a new […] training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).
Note: RLCD rhymes with the “traditional” methods:
- RLHF: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback
- RLVR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
They even claim:
Jev is neither small nor an LLM, hence being off the intelligence Pareto curve.
Fortunately, there’s no shortage of similar models, some of them with even better performance (Laya, Kev, Nimble, NanoJev, etc.)
So let me sum up the marketing strategy:
- Name dropping: former ChatGPT creator, Jevons’ paradox, Pareto curve, System one
- Big claim: cannot hallucinate, exponentially faster and cheaper, entirely new stack, amazing benchmarks and demos
- Ambiguity and jargon: no useful implementation details on the “new training algorithm” or RLCD dataset
- Drama: Laya showed this idea in 1.5 years prior to Jev’s launch
OK, I think at this point we’ve seen this pattern enough to recognize it. I actually think Jev’s team kicked it up a notch to a comical level. Whether their marketing is written by LLM or not, they nailed it.
Fortunately, Jev’s initial noise died off almost at the same speed that it blew up. I can only speculate that as more people experimented with it, we realized:
- It cannot hallucinate, but it can still be wrong. It is even more wrong than conventional language models, and in that sense “system one” is the right naming. Although I consider all current generations of language models system one (even the reasoning models) because they do not really reason in the sense that’s expected of system two.
- It is cheaper, but there are open-weight models that beat it in performance/cost ratio (depending on the task). What makes Jev different than frontier-level LLMs is the fact that you can actually run it at the edge (e.g. locally) with matching quality.
Jev is not completely hype, we just went from “Peak of Inflated Expectations” to the “Trough of Disillusionment” in record time:
It’s not dead. Some companies use it while I believe the majority of use cases are addressed by open-weight rivals.
I really don’t want to bash Jev. Instead I want to use it as an example of where we are, as an industry.
Incremental improvements
I was one of the lucky few who got access to GPT-2 when it was invitation-only.
As a senior tech lead, I allocate part of my time to scout new tech and experiment in order to stay relevant. Prior to that, I had experienced IBM Watson and a bunch of other products so it wasn’t a big deal for me personally.
I was actually underwhelmed by GPT-2 because at the time it could:
- Summarize text
- Predict what comes after a piece of text
- … that was it really! 😄 I don’t remember more than that. So I moved on…
Then I saw someone create a turn-based dialogue from one of these models and to spice it up, they added an avatar to it. I thought it was creepy and funny.
Then Blake Lemoine came out claiming Google’s language model named LaMDA was conscious. Unsurprisingly, this started a philosophical discussion that’s still ongoing on the side. Again, I didn’t give it too much thought.
BUT, Sam Altman, having spent a few years at the startup accelerator (Y Combinator), saw an opportunity. Specifically the chat application seems to have got his attention and soon ChatGPT was announced.
At the time, I thought it was a cool way to turn their token prediction model into a user-friendly product for the masses.
Personally, I couldn’t use it seriously because:
- Poor quality: it didn’t know what it didn’t know, so it just winged it (AKA hallucination). Although the rise of “prompt engineering” and “reasoning models” promised to reduce this issue.
- Privacy: I had been working with computers for 2+ decades at the time and live by the mantra that “if it’s possible, assume it happened”. Meaning if OpenAI is technically capable of storing my conversation, I cannot trust it enough to share any company IP or private information with it.
I vividly remember the backlash Google got for their multi-modal demo when people realized it wasn’t recorded in real-time! Those were the days when even a small deception would be a conspiracy.
When llama.cpp came out I got a gaming machine with an NVIDIA card (AI machines weren’t a thing back then) to build with AI.
Meanwhile people discovered that language models can generate code It was tedious to copy/paste it so we got the early versions of a harness.
Quickly after, we got “function calls” which allowed the models to do stuff!
I was using VS Code at the time and the hype was hard to ignore even though my company at the time had a strict policy against using AI tools (yes! hard to believe that just 3-4 years ago companies prioritized IP over velocity).
I remember paying for a Copilot subscription out of pocket and using VS Code insider on my open source projects.
I was so frustrated that I shared this meme on the company Slack:
Meanwhile there was drama at OpenAI (Ilya was part of a coup that fired their CEO, then Satya was playing 4D chess while Elon was lawyering up). It was a sh*tshow which is exactly how it managed to capture the interest of non-techies, a trend that continues to today with “almighty rogue AI” hacking others while whistle-blowers and alarmists rise speak of existential threat!
Simultaneously premature AI products were creating dramas of their own (assisting crimes, cheating, etc.) and AI bros anthropomorphize the tool as if it had desires of its own (my read: they want to judge accountability).
There’s also circular investment, pentagon drama, chip wars, autonomous killer drones, etc. but in the spirit of brevity, let’s stick to the technical side of things.
Then Peter Steinberger, a veteran developer who was away from computers due to burnout, created an AI companion, which brought the Agents (LM that can do stuff) to the mainstream.
So far I’ve covered:
- Instruction-tuned models
- Function calls
- Coding harnesses
- AI agents
Let’s speed through the other incremental improvements:
- Larger parameter size unlocks emergent properties that are hard to explain by analyzing the micro level architecture (mostly leading to sophisticated perceived behavior but also jagged alignment).
- Larger context windows improve accuracy (although the practical limit is much smaller than the theoretical size).
- Multimodal models enable generating voice, music, pictures, and videos while increasingly more models can understand these modalities.
- MCP abstracts away the implementation and enables different AI products to use the tools needed to do productive work.
- ACP, sub-agents and various orchestration techniques allow larger tasks to be planned and broken into smaller pieces.
- Sandboxes help improve security and isolate unwanted side effects of agentic workflows and when they fall short, there’s HITL (but we still haven’t solved the approval fatigue).
- Skills, web search and web access allow agents to access information that’s outside their training data or knowledge cut-off date.
- Various memory architectures and consolidation techniques enable the models to recall what they learn.
- Chinese labs showed us more efficient ways to train and run the models.
- Feedback loops and scratchpads improve the model’s perceived quality by running part of the verification closer to the model.
This is good progress, no question about it. But I think a part of the reason AI is a hot topic is all the drama surrounding it:
- Geopolitics: unlike the US economy which is primarily service-based, China is a manufacturing behemoth. Up until DeepSeek discovered that it can manipulate stock and AI investment by diffusing the compute equation, I don’t think China had a solid AI plan. Now they do. Good old American sanctions target their chip import but China (being run by engineers) made huge strides recently both in chip manufacturing but also in model architecture. Meanwhile AI is used in warfare from drones to intelligence (and mass surveillance back home). In the best seller How the mighty falls, Collins lists 5 stages of demise: a) Hubris Born of Success, b) Undisciplined Pursuit of More, c) Denial of Risk and Peril, d) Grasping for Salvation, e) Capitulation to Irrelevance or Death. Those same stages apply to a falling empires and in this case US has bet big on AI while China diffuses US’s massive bet with open-weight models. Consumers win for now.
- Debt bubble: You can read more on Bloomberg but it basically boils down to a series of interdependent bets that is so large it impacts the national GDP. It has to work regardless of how much IP has to be stolen and how many lies have to be told. The stakes are too high at this point.
- Safety: we got used to the “rogue AI” narrative where the AI vendors aren’t held accountable for breaking into other companies and government institutes. Why would we? It’s an open secret that the training data wasn’t legally obtained anyway (and there are multiple class action lawsuits to prove that). On top of it, there have been multiple cases where people lost their lives due to AI — and I’m not even counting “vibe war”. (yes, I actually put an em-dash there!) 🙃
- Impact on jobs: software engineering is low-hanging fruit for AI automation due to its nature (there’s plenty of training data, and the tools are often on a language model’s home turf). There have been discussions of UBI (universal basic income) and UHI (universal high income) but looking at the benevolence of the billionaires running the show, I don’t buy it at all.
AI is hot, because it can potentially impact all of us. But we have to remember one simple fact:
Humans are fundamentally flawed when it comes to predicting the future.
Most notoriously, we have difficulty understanding the S-curve (meaning the pace of change is slow at the beginning and end).
And with prominent scientists leaving their lucrative positions to slow down the pace of development, we really cannot be sure about how long it will take for AI to really manifest the changes, if ever.
What’s missing?
With all the incremental improvements of the past few years, we still haven’t solved some fundamental problems.
Here’s a short list of what I consider truly game changing:
- Abstract reasoning: neural networks (not just language models) are prone to making stuff up (hallucination). The state of the industry has improved a lot since hands had 5+ fingers and videos were easy to detect, but the closest we’ve come to a true system 2 is to pair the models with code and still the feedback loops and human intervention are necessary.
- Continuous learning: auxiliary context (e.g. skills, grounding, search and various model architectures) has come a long way but we’re far from the state where the models learn in real time. By extension, the next generation of AI should learn from fewer samples, data and repetitions.
- Embodiment: while there have been great improvements in robotic body form factor, we’re still not at a point where AI is rapid and efficient enough to be put in a robot body and react to the sensory stimuli in real time or expose fine motoric control and navigate the 3D world with enough prevision to take over “simple” human chores.
- Economics of running AI: Jensen Huang talks about installing “Gigawatts” of compute as if it’s normal to measure temperature in kilometers/hour!!! The truth is: our brain delivers AGI level intelligence at 20 Watts and until we solve that problem, there is not enough water, power and data centers that can realistically make massive change in workforce. Unfortunately, we live in a post-truth world where hysteria, personalized propaganda and mass psychosis have an oversized impact on the dominant discourse so we’re all supposed to be scared and distracted. The economics makes even less sense if we expect embodied AI (robots) to replace even a fraction of human population. Unlike bots, our organic bodies return to nature and participate in the nature’s recycling system much faster than metals and plastic that build a robot. Sometimes I feel we forgot that we’re living on a tiny rock with finite resources which get increasingly harder to extract.
All of this, is not to say that AI won’t be used to:
- Robosoldiers and robocops
- Generate new diseases
- Connect mass surveillance to personalized propaganda
- Corporate espionage and mass penetration into computer systems
- etc.
The truth is: you don’t need AGI-level of intelligence to cause destruction. The current generation of AI, paired with harness, tools and skills is plenty capable of causing damage in the wrong hands.
And if you think this is not happening already, I know a guy who gives free ice cream in his basement! 🙃
Recap
I think Jev is a good example of how great marketing fizzed out in the face of reality.
- Is it useful? Yes.
- Is it relevant? Yes.
- Is it dead? Just its hype.
- Is it revolutionary? Depends on your cost, quality, speed triangle.
- Is it as big as it was claimed? I hope you have the answer by now.
If I had a magic wand, I would want us all to step back and see the holistic arc of recent events and calm down a little. The red flags are easy to see:
- Name dropping: builds a bridge between the new unknown to the trusted known.
- Jargon: makes you feel stupid for not having the context.
- Ambiguity: lets your brain fill in the blanks and if you’re an optimist, you’re at risk of getting overly excited and eventually disappointed
- Inflate expectations: big claims require big evidence. Don’t trust the isolated benchmarks that do not resemble how YOU would actually use it, especially if the benchmark is coming from the same entity that has a conflict of interest.
- Drama: engages human emotion to what would otherwise be a logical technical decision. “All publicity is good publicity”.
Unfortunately, I think that ship might have already sailed and in the age of mass-produced synthetic content and personalized propaganda, maybe we’re too stressed to think straight.
Maybe LLMs are “system two”, after all, if we collectively lose our critical thinking and let our emotions be manipulated with the kind of marketing and manipulation we’ve seen too much lately.
Someone shared this on Hackernews (thank you 🙌) and it went all the way up to 2nd spot.
The early comments came at agentic speed and were unanimously focused on two things: 1) anecdotes about Jev being alive, and conveniently ignoring competition, 2) taking it personal and making it personal as if killing the messenger will make the message false. Weird. 🤔
My monetization strategy is to give away most content for free but these posts take anywhere from a few hours to a few days to draft, edit, research, illustrate, and publish. I pull these hours from my private time, vacation days and weekends. The simplest way to support this work is to like, subscribe and share it. If you really want to support me in lifting our community, you can consider a paid subscription. If you want to save, you can get 20% off via this link. As a token of appreciation, subscribers get full access to the Pro-Tips sections and my online book Reliability Engineering Mindset. Your contribution also funds my open-source products like Service Level Calculator. You can also invite your friends to gain free access or save via a group subscription.
And to those of you who already support me, thank you for sponsoring this content for the others. 🙌 If you have questions or feedback, or you want me to dig deeper into something, please let me know in the comments.
results.summary:
The rapid rise and fall of the Jev AI model highlights a broader industry trend of using aggressive marketing and technical jargon to inflate expectations for incremental innovations.

### Key Points
- Jev is a general-purpose classifier marketed as a "System One" decision model, though it lacks the reasoning capabilities of advanced language models.
- The product launch relied on high-profile associations with ChatGPT creators and complex terminology like "Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions" (RLCD).
- Despite claims of being a revolutionary breakthrough, Jev faces stiff competition from existing open-weight models that offer superior performance-to-cost ratios.
- The hype cycle surrounding Jev mirrors a recurring pattern in the AI sector where dramatic announcements often mask a lack of significant technical differentiation.
- Fundamental challenges in AI, such as true abstract reasoning, continuous real-time learning, and energy-efficient embodiment, remain largely unsolved.

### Why it Matters
The Jev hype cycle serves as a case study for how manipulative marketing and industry drama can distract from the reality of slow, incremental progress in artificial intelligence. Investors and users must look past the jargon to distinguish between genuine technological breakthroughs and products designed to capitalize on current market hysteria.

results.title: The next-gen Xbox won’t cost you $1,800. It can’t. Can it?
results.author: Sean Hollister
results.content:
Fortune dropped a bombshell report on the future of gaming this week. According to the publication’s Microsoft insiders, the next Xbox is projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 when it arrives in 2028.
The next-gen Xbox won’t cost you $1,800. It can’t. Can it?
Didn’t Microsoft say the next Xbox needed to be affordable?
My first reaction: The next Xbox is dead on arrival. It’s DOA.
My second thought: Microsoft knows people won’t pay that much. It couldn’t possibly charge that much money if it wants next gen to be a success. “I wouldn’t release it at all,” former Microsoft exec Mike Ybarra recently said.
My third thought: Didn’t Microsoft already say out loud that it knows people won’t pay that much?
- Didn’t old Xbox boss Phil Spencer say “We’re not going to grow the market with $1,000 consoles”?
- Didn’t new Xbox boss Asha Sharma say “We’ve reached a point where it will be hard to imagine that mass audiences can afford thousands of dollars to spend” on a box?
- Didn’t Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball say the entire company would change its practices to make sure it’s affordable?
- Didn’t Sharma say Xbox would need to adopt “radically different business models” to keep Xbox from being too pricey?
Did Fortune get it wrong?
I don’t think Fortune’s insiders are the problem here. With today’s incredibly overpriced RAM and storage, it wouldn’t be surprising if it cost over a thousand dollars to build, package, distribute, and sell “the largest technical leap you will have ever seen in a hardware generation,” as former Xbox president Sarah Bond called the next Xbox back in 2024.
But there are at least five ways the report could be correct without making you pay all that money at once. I just don’t think you’re going to like most of them.
Subsidies: Microsoft could pay to give you a discount
The least-likely possibility is the one Fortune suggests itself. Let’s look at the original quote, bolding mine:
[…] the price of the Helix console has internally been projected to cost consumers between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost.
Historically, Microsoft has subsidized the Xbox. Microsoft sold boxes at a loss right out of the gate, making its profits when you buy games and Xbox Game Pass subscriptions instead of on the hardware alone. That’s not our speculation — it’s exactly what Microsoft told The Verge in 2021. In 2023, we learned that Microsoft may have spent $1.5 billion to make sure it could sell the Xbox Series X and S at $499 and $299 respectively, instead of what they actually cost.
But Microsoft has suggested that it’s done with hardware subsidies. “Going forward, this cannot continue,” wrote Sharma in her “Xbox reset” memo, referring to the $20 billion in content, platform, and hardware subsidies Microsoft made over the past five years.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed that idea on the Hard Fork podcast: “No one can accuse Microsoft of not having invested for the last 25 years, and now we have to turn this into a sustainable business.”
It isn’t just new management that’s hinting at no more subsidies: Bond primed the pump for a $1,000 box when she called Helix “a very premium, very high-end curated experience” late last year, comparing it to gaming PCs like the $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld.
Perhaps Microsoft has changed its mind since then. “We are working very hard to rethink everything that we can about Helix,” Ball said in June, referring to affordability. “The plan’s the plan until it’s not the plan,” Sharma said in February (though not about affordability specifically).
But subsidies would be a tremendous risk if the Helix still plays PC games in addition to Xbox ones. Valve’s Steam is by far the dominant PC gaming platform — so PC gamers who buy a Helix won’t help Microsoft recoup its money.
Subscription: “Get it free with 36 months of Xbox Game Pass and qualifying trade-in”
There’s another way Microsoft could subsidize a $1,200 Xbox.
Today, AT&T will give you a $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro for $0* — if you lock yourself into 36 months of AT&T phone service that costs $100 or more per month and trade in a recent phone, too.
Microsoft could do the same with a new, pricier tier of its Xbox Game Pass game subscription service, effectively bundling the games with the console and making you slowly pay for both at the same time. Perhaps you’ll have the option to buy an “unlocked” Xbox for full price, but it won’t be the norm.
To make it happen directly, Microsoft would need a pricier new tier of Xbox Game Pass, which wouldn’t necessarily align with the company’s recent moves. Sharma actually cut the price of Game Pass Ultimate to $22.99 a month in April, writing that “Game Pass has become too expensive for players,” while removing Call of Duty games and unlimited access to Xbox Cloud Gaming from the deal.
I don’t know if it would work. People feel naked leaving the house without phone service. They might not feel the same about games. Subscription fatigue is real. But if it worked, Microsoft’s moat would be stronger than ever. You’ll be more likely to play the games you’ve already paid for and are committed to keep paying for. Many would get sucked into a profitable upgrade cycle, just like they do with phones, since they can buy the next Xbox for “$0” as soon as it comes out.
Cellphone subsidies have been around nearly as long as pricey phones: The 1994 IBM Simon, arguably the first smartphone, eventually cost half its $1,100 price tag if you signed a contract with BellSouth. My first phone, a Kyocera QCP-6035 with a built-in PalmPilot, was subsidized when it arrived in 2001. So it’s not exactly a “radical new business model,” but it would be new for game consoles.
Rental: Maybe most people won’t own a Helix themselves
It’s also possible that Microsoft simply doesn’t plan to sell a console to the masses anymore — it can sell an $1,800 Xbox to those who can afford “video game ownership” and try to hook everyone else on the Netflix model.
After all, the “K-shaped economy” and RAMageddon have already made gaming PCs and existing game consoles into luxury goods. Society’s wealthier individuals seem perfectly happy to pay inflated prices for the few consoles Sony and Microsoft still pump out.
While PS5 sales plummeted after Sony’s price hikes, that may have been about component shortages rather than decreased demand. Xbox sales reportedly rose over a similar period, and Microsoft has justified repeated, dramatic price hikes on its consoles since May 2025.
“I can tell you definitively, demand for our console exceeds supply. We are putting them in as many stores as possible, we are producing them as quickly as possible. There is a severe limitation to how quickly we can do that,” Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball told The Game Business in June, blaming RAM shortages.
But Microsoft has another way of giving less affluent people access to “next-gen” Xbox power. It can rent you one. The company just launched pay-as-you-go cloud gaming starting at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud gaming (50 hours for $11.99).
Maybe all of Microsoft’s recent talk about affordability isn’t about the masses owning a next-gen console. Maybe it’s about finding an affordable way for people to “play Xbox” without owning the games at all.
The next gen is the current gen
After Fortune’s report, some of the very first reactions I saw boiled down to this: “I’m out. Forget next gen, I’m going to stick with my existing Xbox/PlayStation/Switch.”
That’ll be the reality for many people if the Xbox costs over a thousand bucks. But if the RAM shortage continues — if Microsoft knows it’ll sell every Xbox it can make to wealthy individuals because it can’t make a lot — it’s not necessarily a huge risk to sell it sky-high on day one.
Perhaps the Xbox Helix will be an early adopter console, the same way the iPhone Duo is an early adopter phone, the same way the Steam Frame is an early adopter headset. These products are selling out instantly despite their high price tags, leaving many would-be buyers in the cold. They’re shipping messy and unfinished, but that’s okay because early adopters want to come along for the ride.
Microsoft knows the same is true of some Xbox buyers, because it helped ship an unfinished $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld even before the RAM crisis, and the $1,300 Xbox Ally X20 follow-up is already sold out.
But if Microsoft splits the Xbox audience into “have” and “have-not,” it means the next generation won’t truly arrive. Game developers won’t spend all their effort targeting a console people can’t buy. The next Xbox won’t be any more necessary than a PS5 Pro if you already own a PS5. In industry lingo, the Helix would be a “mid-cycle refresh” instead of true next gen.
I wouldn’t hate that, though, and neither would many video game execs. They’ve long complained that the pace of technology has ballooned the cost of building a video game to unsustainable levels, leading to today’s world where too many development teams are cut to the bone right after their games ship.
Former PlayStation and Xbox execs like Shuhei Yoshida, Shawn Layden, and Mike Ybarra have argued that the next gen isn’t necessary.
“Stick with PS5 Pro/Series X until prices normalize. The capabilities of those boxes are both fine for 99% of the audience. No one is screaming ‘I need a more powerful console’ right now,” Ybarra tweeted on October 20th.
“I think [Sony and Nintendo] should try to keep the current generation as long as possible, because I think people are very happy using PS5 and Switch 2,” Yoshida told me on The Vergecast.
“I think we’ve plateaued on the tech, frankly,” Layden told GamesIndustry.biz in 2025. (He’s said similar before and since.) “Make it cheaper and simpler. Let’s do that instead. And let’s find a way to have more hardware companies participate.”
Microsoft and its chip partner AMD have already taken one step to help extend the current generation — AMD’s performance-enhancing FSR 4.1 is coming to Xbox Series S and X, which should make it easier for both to deliver crisp 4K images to your TV.
Pay what you can afford
Even if Microsoft ships a $1,800 console, the company’s been clear it won’t be the only Xbox you can buy. Sharma has publicly said that Helix will be a “family of devices,” which has been broadly interpreted to mean that Microsoft will let PC industry partners like Asus sell their own “Xbox” as well.
If the reporting pans out, that wouldn’t just be a cobranded Xbox Ally handheld that runs Windows — Asus could make a console-shaped box that runs a Windows-based Xbox OS, too.
Some of those partners could offer more affordable, less powerful Xboxes than Microsoft’s own flagship box, perhaps with less storage and memory. Microsoft, too, might have creative solutions for storage, like how the company shipped the Xbox 360 with different-size hard drives, or none at all, to make it more affordable. “We will have to empower customers to have very flexible storage offerings,” Sharma said in June.
Or you could buy another Xbox that’s likely going to continue to count as part of Microsoft’s “family”: the existing Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S.
This can all work because games don’t need to target a single console anymore; they haven’t needed to for a long time. An Xbox One game runs on an Xbox One X and an Xbox Series S and an Xbox Series X because they’re all effectively AMD-powered Windows PCs, just with different amounts of performance on tap. The Xbox Helix is a powerful extension of the same continuum. The same is true of PlayStation 4, PS4 Pro, PS5, PS5 Pro, and presumably PS6, minus the Windows part.
Perhaps a particular piece of hardware will stand out as the one developers should target as the baseline for “it looks and runs great on Xbox,” the same way the Steam Deck handheld became a baseline for PC game developers starting in 2022. Maybe, like the Steam Deck and the Nintendo Switch, it’ll help reset our expectations of what a top-shelf game needs to look like.
At this rate, I wouldn’t be surprised if the existing Xbox Series S will be the one. But it could also be Microsoft’s own next handheld Xbox. Fortune’s insiders say it’s coming holiday 2027.
results.summary:
**Microsoft’s upcoming "Helix" console could retail between $1,200 and $1,800 by 2028, forcing the company to consider new business models to maintain affordability for its mass-market gaming audience.**

### Key Points
- Reports suggest the next-generation Xbox, codenamed "Helix," may carry a premium price tag due to rising costs for high-end RAM and storage components.
- Microsoft executives, including Asha Sharma and Phil Spencer, have previously acknowledged that mass-market consumers cannot afford multi-thousand-dollar gaming hardware.
- Potential strategies to offset costs include bundling the console with long-term Xbox Game Pass subscriptions or shifting toward cloud-based rental models.
- The "Helix" is expected to be part of a broader "family of devices," potentially allowing third-party partners like Asus to release more affordable, varied hardware options.
- Industry experts suggest that current-generation consoles like the Xbox Series X and S may remain relevant longer as developers focus on scaling games across diverse hardware tiers.

### Why it Matters
The potential shift toward a high-priced, premium console signals a fundamental change in how Microsoft approaches the gaming market, moving away from traditional hardware subsidies. By diversifying its hardware ecosystem and emphasizing subscription services, the company aims to balance the high cost of cutting-edge technology with the need to keep gaming accessible to a wider audience.

results.title: A New Bird-Recognizing Feeder Under $100 Launches for Beginner Bird-Watchers
results.author: Tyler Lacoma
results.content:
Birdbuddy released its latest line of smart bird feeders equipped with cameras that can detect birds by species on Thursday, and it’s never been a better time to start birdwatching at your home. The reason is a new model called the Birdbuddy Nook, which starts at $99 and offers its AI features for free with no subscription needed.
Read more: The Best Smart Bird Feeders, Tested and Reviewed
Most of the smart bird feeders we’ve tested, including past Birdbuddy models, cost around $200 or more. The particularly affordable Nook includes a 2K-resolution camera with both portrait and landscape orientations, plus a 3.8-cup birdseed container. It wakes up via motion but can keep recording for longer periods of time when there’s lots of activity. All the alerts and species recognition features happen on your phone, via the Birdbuddy app.
More from CNET
The Nook comes in both a standard model for $99 and a model with a solar panel built into the roof for $159. I’ve tested many solar-powered security cameras, and these small panels really do help keep wireless batteries charged for long periods. Since the Nook’s battery is only rated for around a month, and the bird-feeder battery looks a bit more complicated to charge up, I highly recommend the solar model.
Along with the Nook, the company is releasing a Birdbuddy Home mode for $219, which is similar, except it has a larger 6-cup capacity and a wraparound bar for more perching space.
Where should you put the Nook?
Feeders should be placed within 4 feet to 10 feet of shrubs or trees, which is close enough for birds to feel safe from predators, while still being far enough to deter squirrels, according to Mary Mack Gray, Birdbuddy’s in-house ornithologist, who told CNET the best placement options. “If using a pole, a height of 5 to 6 feet off the ground is ideal. Nook is designed for compact spaces like patios, balconies and small yards.”
If you’re worried about squirrels messing up your view or getting in the way, Gray suggests using safflower seeds and suet, which squirrels tend to ignore, and avoid feed like corn or peanuts that squirrels love.
How does the bird recognition feature work?
Birdbuddy uses AI that has been trained on bird species visits to feeders, so it can analyze shape, color, markings and other aspects to pull up a match if one is available. The camera needs a couple of moments to wake up and take a snapshot, as well as a Wi-Fi connection, so you don’t want to put the feeder out too far from your router.
Once a bird lands on the feeder, the feeder will send a snapshot to algorithms for analysis and return an identified species or label it as currently unknown. Birdbuddy doesn’t say if it’s all local AI or if processing is done in the cloud.
CNET’s previous birdwatching reviewer noted that, aside from an occasional misstep, the bird recognition was quite good and even self-corrected itself. That sounds like a handy package for someone who wants to get to know birds in the area while paying the minimum amount.
results.summary:
Birdbuddy has launched the Nook, an affordable smart bird feeder starting at $99 that features AI-powered species recognition and a 2K camera without requiring a monthly subscription fee.

### Key Points
- The Birdbuddy Nook is available in a standard $99 model and a $159 version featuring an integrated solar panel.
- The device includes a 3.8-cup seed capacity and a 2K-resolution camera capable of recording in both portrait and landscape orientations.
- A larger model, the Birdbuddy Home, offers a 6-cup capacity and expanded perching space for $219.
- AI software identifies bird species by analyzing physical characteristics like color and markings through the Birdbuddy mobile app.
- Ornithologist Mary Mack Gray recommends placing feeders 5 to 6 feet off the ground and 4 to 10 feet from nearby shrubs.

### Why it Matters
This release significantly lowers the entry price for smart birdwatching technology, which typically costs upwards of $200. By removing subscription requirements for AI features, Birdbuddy is positioning its hardware as a more accessible consumer option for backyard nature enthusiasts.

results.title: That's a problem: Galaxy S26 Ultra suffers a horrendous setup bug after One UI 9
results.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
results.content:
What you need to know
- After updating to One UI 9, a Korean user states they've encountered a critical setup bug.
- The user is unable to view their lock screen or home screen with this bug, but Samsung was quick to respond.
- They were encouraged to update their browser and to connect to Wi-Fi, not their cellular service.
The last thing anyone wants is a software bug that completely kneecaps their device. Unfortunately, that's exactly what some Galaxy S26 Ultra users are experiencing.
A user on Samsung's Korean forums says their Galaxy S26 Ultra is experiencing a critical error after updating to One UI 9 (via SammyFans). They state in their report (machine-translated), "Since the UI 9.0 update, this keeps appearing on my phone screen. The screen is black and the home screen isn't appearing either." What they're referring to is an error message that reads, "The webpage is unavailable... for the following reasons."
As the user states, they're unable to get past this startup screen after downloading Samsung's major Android OS upgrade. The only good news is that Samsung was quick to respond to their report. According to Samsung, "The development team has confirmed that this issue occurs when using an unstable system WebView on certain networks. We kindly ask that you follow the troubleshooting guide below."
The company suggests updating your browser, such as Google Chrome. It also recommends switching to a Wi-Fi network, not your phone's cell service. Once that's done, users can try logging into their Samsung Account as normal.
There's a chance this bug could get fixed in a future software update, but Samsung hasn't confirmed that yet.
Not a good look
This problem seems quite specific. Right now, it's unclear how widespread the problem is. However, One UI 9 hasn't been all roses for Galaxy users. Users on Reddit reported an "XML Access Denied error" almost two weeks ago (via Android Police). This error reportedly froze users' devices, which seems to have impacted the Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy S24, and others.
One user had to remove their SIM card in order to proceed, while another found relief by booting in safe mode with their Wi-Fi connection off.

We've been met with nothing but delays; however, in late September, the Galaxy S26 series finally got it in the U.S. T-Mobile customers reportedly got it first with a 4GB download. Shortly after, others received it for their respective carriers (or unlocked version).
Over the past few weeks, the update has rolled out for several budget phones, the Galaxy S25, and S24 series.

I've seen similar frustrations amongst users online when it comes to problems with Samsung's updates. We wait so long for them, go through delays, and then there's a major bug like this. results.title: Palmer Luckey Made a Genetically Modified Military Dog Startup
results.author: Kate Knibbs
results.content:
A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.
Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm. The startup has raised $200 million to “rebuild America’s domestic supply of elite working dogs” and reduce dependency on European dog breeders for military canines.
Lamm tells WIRED that Warhound is in the process of gene-editing its first batch of dogs. The startup has already collected blood samples from specific "top-performing” military, police, and first responder dogs in the United States, and its goal is to clone them. Breeds will be “mostly Belgian Malinois, some labs, and some shepherds,” he says. The company anticipates the first round of puppies to be born in early 2027.
The initial rounds of gene-editing will focus on eliminating common health conditions that impact these breeds, like hip dysplasia. Further down the line, Lamm envisions expanding to “really interesting things,” such as incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to “enhance” the military dogs. (Colossal Biosciences is perhaps best known for its work on gene-edited wolves for its so-called Dire Wolf De-Extinction Project.)
Warhound, based in Texas, will also equip its canines with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to a press release. Asked if this means the dogs will be some kind of cyborgs, Lamm clarifies that the plan right now is to supply them with tools like “advanced body armor” rather than, say, embedding some sort of computer in their dog bodies.
“So no dogs with lasers?” WIRED asked Lamm.
“I can’t comment on what Anduril plans,” he says. “Dog safety and performance, and then helping continue helping to improve the human handler and dog bond, and working as a team—that is what the mission is.”
Neither Luckey nor Lamm will be involved in Warhound’s day-to-day, although Lamm is on the company’s board, he says. David Spirk, a former Department of Defense chief data officer who most recently worked at Palantir, is serving as chief executive, and investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest. Luckey is not an owner and does not have equity in the company, nor does Anduril; Colossal Biosciences does have an ownership stake.
Luckey and Lamm have been working on the project for over a year, Lamm says, and just recently decided to take the company out of stealth. “Someone said, ‘So it's like the Captain America dog program with the Ironman tech program on top of it,’” Lamm tells WIRED.
Everyone can agree that this is normal, and good, and that when the precision-designed beasts arrive on Earth, they will recognize that we are not the enemy.
The company plans to operate under the guidance of the American Humane Society.
results.summary:
Texas-based startup Warhound has raised $200 million to develop genetically enhanced working dogs for military and emergency services, with the first puppies expected to arrive in early 2027.

### Key Points
- Warhound was co-founded by Ben Lamm and supported by Palmer Luckey to reduce U.S. reliance on European dog breeders.
- The company plans to clone top-performing Belgian Malinois, Labradors, and shepherds while using gene-editing to eliminate hereditary health issues.
- Future development may include incorporating wolf DNA to enhance olfactory capabilities and integrating advanced body armor and situational awareness technology.
- Former Department of Defense official David Spirk will serve as CEO, with backing from investors including In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest.
- Operations will be conducted under the guidance of the American Humane Society to ensure animal safety and performance standards.

### Why it Matters
This initiative represents a significant shift toward integrating biotechnology and advanced hardware into the domestic defense supply chain. By creating a specialized, genetically optimized canine workforce, the project could fundamentally change how military and emergency agencies approach field operations and handler-animal partnerships.
