results.title: Apple is finally catching up with Siri, but the goalposts are moving again
results.author: Marcus Mendes
results.content:
9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: Memoket Gem is a 0.4 oz AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch. One press captures a conversation, and KITE memory connects it to what you said weeks ago. 20-hour battery. Available now from $168.99 on memoket.ai and Amazon.
While it is great that Siri AI can finally deliver Apple’s promise of an actually useful, personal assistant for the age of AI, expectations surrounding agentic assistants are quickly shifting. But Apple is showing it might not watch from the sidelines again.
Siri AI is great, but it’s also very 2024
Now that Siri AI (which is still officially designated as a beta) has been out for a little more than a month, it seems fair to say that its two defining characteristics are that it’s finally useful, but it can be painfully slow to answer even simple queries.
And while I had spent the better part of the past few months mocking Silicon Valley’s obsession with AI assistants that can book flights and hotels, I hate to admit that the first time Siri AI actually impressed me was when I asked how much I’d paid for a hotel room for an upcoming trip to San Francisco and how far it was from my first appointment in the city. It got both answers exactly right.
Could I have looked this up myself? Sure. But setting aside the fact that I was in the middle of a 10K run at the time, finding that information on my own would undoubtedly have taken longer than it took Siri to give me the answers.
As a result, over the past few months, I’ve found myself increasingly relying on Siri AI for questions like “What was the contact information for that plumber who fixed the kitchen sink leak a couple of years ago?” or “What was the name of that PR person who introduced me to so-and-so?”
Information I know I have somewhere, be it an iMessage conversation or an email receipt, and that although I could just search for it, I’d now rather have Siri AI do it for me.
And for the first time in 15 years, I can ask these questions without already expecting Siri to fail halfway through asking them, only to get frustrated when it inevitably gets it wrong and proves me right.
That’s all well and good. The problem is that Apple has only now caught up with what AI assistants could do in 2024.
Apple’s next AI challenge: Building an agent harness for Siri
Particularly over the past few months, the frontier AI market has increasingly shifted toward agentic assistants, with products from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and xAI (among many others) moving beyond answering questions to actually carrying out tasks on users’ behalf.
I subscribe to ChatGPT, and I’ve been using Codex and ChatGPT Work extensively for everyday tasks involving files and information scattered across my Mac and various cloud services.
And it still feels like magic every time I ask one of these tools to do something that involves opening, creating, editing, or organizing files on my computer, as well as interacting with websites and services I’m logged into, and it actually pulls it off.
The flipside of this is that every time ChatGPT completes one such task, the new Siri AI starts to feel like the old Siri all over again.
It is still early days, for sure, but it already feels like this is yet another area where Apple seems to be falling increasingly behind, as AI labs continue to improve their agentic capabilities, sometimes rolling out major updates just weeks apart, while Apple remains largely tied to its annual software release cycle.
But there’s one important limitation to today’s agentic assistants that I think Apple is particularly well positioned to address.
As impressive as tools like Codex, Dots, and ChatGPT Work can be, they still depend heavily on the user to provide the permissions and the context behind whatever task they’re supposed to accomplish. They can access files, search through emails, and interact with websites, but they generally don’t know what you’re doing, what you’ve been discussing with other people, or what you might need next unless you explicitly tell them.
And as these tools become increasingly capable of operating our computers and phones on our behalf, I suspect the next big leap in their usefulness will come not just from improving what they can do, but from improving their proactive understanding of the user’s context in real time.
That’s where Apple could have an advantage.
Apple has recently shown that it’s finally willing to capitalize on the trust it has spent years building around privacy, even if it means testing the boundaries of what users are comfortable sharing with an AI assistant.
Last month, it introduced two Apple Watch features: Siri Recap, which can automatically generate summaries of conversations throughout the day, and Live Rewind, which lets users retrieve the last 15 seconds of a conversation they may have missed.
Both features rely on the Apple Watch’s microphone to capture information about what’s happening around the user, potentially giving Siri access to an entirely new source of personal context.
Of course, the privacy implications are enormous, particularly because conversations involve other people who haven’t necessarily agreed to have their words processed by an AI assistant.
And while those concerns are certainly worth discussing at length (and are probably why these features have yet to roll out), Apple has repeatedly shown that it’s willing to go to extraordinary lengths to address the privacy challenges that come with giving technology access to sensitive personal information. Just look at the lengths it went to in developing its Reference Image system.
As agentic assistants become more capable, I suspect their biggest limitation will increasingly have less to do with what the underlying models can do, and more with how much we’re willing to let them know about us.
Imagine an assistant that doesn’t just wait for you to ask it to find a document or complete a task, but already understands what you’re working on. One that can gather information in the background so it’s ready when you need it, or even take action on your behalf based on what’s happening around you.
That’s the kind of assistant that could make today’s agentic tools feel as limited as the old Siri (and, increasingly, the new Siri AI) does now.
And while Apple still has plenty of catching up to do when it comes to actually building these capabilities, it is in a much better position to compete in this next phase of AI than it was when the generative AI race first began.
Top comment by Keith B.
I don’t understand 9 to 5’s obsession with claiming that new Siri is better, or getting better. It is definitely worse at doing the things that it always did. It’s slower and fails more often. There are still basic things that it just cannot do. Like play a particular Apple Music station or playlist. It’s extra slow on the Watch. I canceled my HomePod mini 2 order after giving new Siri another try. It doesn’t work the same across devices, like Apple said that it would.
Apple just added voice recording and note-taking to iPhone and Apple Watch. Useful, but check your battery at 2pm. Dedicated recording is one of the fastest ways to drain a Watch, and your iPhone needs to be out and unlocked to do it. More importantly, neither device connects what was said in today’s meeting to a decision you made three weeks ago. They capture moments. They don’t build memory.
Memoket Gem was built to do more. A 0.4 oz wearable AI agent that slots alongside your Apple Watch on the same wrist. One button, one press, 20 hours of battery. Gem captures conversations and connects them across time using KITE, a long-term memory engine that links what was said today to what mattered weeks ago. When a topic comes back up, Gem surfaces the original conversation automatically. Everything flows into ChatGPT, Claude, Slack, and Notion.
153 languages supported. Available now on memoket.ai and Amazon from $168.99.
results.summary:
Apple’s updated Siri AI offers improved utility for personal information retrieval, yet the company faces increasing pressure to develop agentic capabilities that match competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

### Key Points
- Apple’s Siri AI has improved at retrieving personal data from emails and messages, though users report issues with slow response times and inconsistent performance.
- The broader AI market is shifting toward agentic assistants capable of actively managing files, websites, and tasks across various software platforms.
- Apple is exploring deeper contextual awareness through features like Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which utilize microphone data to summarize daily conversations.
- Privacy remains a significant hurdle for Apple as it attempts to balance advanced data collection with its established reputation for user security.
- The Memoket Gem, a 0.4 oz wearable device, offers an alternative by using a long-term memory engine to link current conversations with past interactions.

### Why it Matters
The transition from simple voice assistants to proactive, agentic AI represents the next major competitive frontier in the technology industry. Apple’s ability to leverage its unique ecosystem and privacy-focused reputation may determine whether it can successfully challenge more agile AI labs in this evolving market.

results.title: AI Benchmark Scores Don’t Tell the Whole Story. Here’s What You Need to Look For.
results.author: Karthigan Vijey
results.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared that “AGI has arrived” after OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra launch, but OpenAI itself never made that claim, and researchers call the term “jagged” rather than general.
- Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 post near identical scores on several benchmarks, yet produce noticeably different real world output. The gap traces back to the “harness” wrapped around the model, not the model itself.
- SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Cursor shows where the real competitive fight is moving. It’s not the raw model anymore. It’s who controls the layer around it.
AGI, artificial general intelligence, means a system that can match or beat human performance across essentially any cognitive task, not just the narrow ones it was trained for. That distinction matters because it’s exactly what’s being argued about right now.
Jensen Huang has a habit of declaring victory at the exact moment his company needs the market to believe it. So when OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra on Sept. 3, Huang posted on X that “AGI has arrived,” adding that “400K GPUs” are “coming online next.”
I’m an AI engineer, and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I spent the last year watching every model release get relabeled as the one that finally changes everything. Here is the truth.
What Astra actually does
Astra isn’t a chatbot upgrade. OpenAI positions it as an operator — a system that browses, codes, runs multi-step workflows, models in Blender and handles cybersecurity tasks with minimal supervision. The benchmark numbers are genuinely striking: 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4, 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3, and a perfect 100% on ExploitBench, up from 78.5% for its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol. Those are not incremental gains.
But OpenAI itself, notably, stopped short of calling Astra AGI, choosing instead to emphasize “speed and versatility.” That restraint from the company that built the model is the tell.
Why people aren’t convinced
The pushback isn’t really about whether Astra is impressive. It clearly is. It’s about the word AGI itself. Wharton professor Ethan Mollick has argued for months that what we’re seeing is “jagged AGI:” systems that are superhuman in some narrow domains and unreliable in others, which is a very different thing from general intelligence.
There’s still no agreed upon test for AGI, so declaring it “arrived” is closer to a subjective judgment call than a measurement. Augmented Mind and Manolo Remiddi put it plainly: “AGI is the point where you can trust the output without checking. We are not there.”
The Fable 5.1 comparison and why scores lie
This is where it gets interesting for anyone actually building with these models. On paper, Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 look neck and neck on several coding and reasoning benchmarks. In practice, engineers report meaningfully different output quality. Fable tends to produce more production-ready code with fewer output tokens, while Astra’s strength shows up more in computer use and multi-step automation. Snorkel AI’s testing revealed that Fable fails through a fundamentally different pattern than how it succeeds, losing valid work mid-trajectory rather than running out of budget, which matters far more to a shipping team than a leaderboard percentage.
The reason similar scores can hide such different outputs comes down to something most people outside AI engineering have never heard of: the harness.
What a “harness” actually is
A harness is the infrastructure wrapped around a model: the prompt assembly, tool access, memory management and error recovery that determine how the raw model is actually put to work. As MindStudio describes it: “A model is the engine. The harness is the car. Most benchmarks test the car.” Swap the harness and the same model produces wildly different results. Cursor’s own research found one model scoring 46% accuracy with one harness and 80% with another, with no model change at all.
Astra’s own benchmark history makes the point better than any explainer could. On ARC-AGI-3, Astra scored 62.7% using a standard harness, essentially tied with its predecessor, and 99.9% using a “Provider Adapter” harness that let it retain and reuse prior reasoning instead of restarting cold on every step, according to Augmented Mind and Manolo Remiddi. Same weights. Same model. A 37 point swing from infrastructure alone. That’s not a small footnote. It means a huge share of what gets reported as “model improvement” is actually harness improvement, and leaderboards that don’t control for it are telling a story, not reporting a fact.
Why Cursor just became the most important acquisition of the year
This is exactly why SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Cursor matters more than it looks. Cursor isn’t a model company. It’s one of the best harness companies in the world, the layer that decides how coding models actually get used. Folding it into SpaceX’s GPU fleet is a bet that owning the layer is as valuable as owning the model, maybe more. OpenAI has already cut Cursor’s access to its models over trust concerns tied to Musk’s companies, which tells you the model providers see the same thing: Whoever controls the harness controls the product experience, regardless of which model sits underneath it.
The bottom line
Nobody serious disputes that GPT-6 Astra is a major model. What’s contested is the leap from “major model” to “AGI has arrived.” If you’re evaluating these systems for your own business, ignore the AGI framing entirely. Look at the harness a vendor wraps around the model, ask how it fails, and test it on your actual workflow. The benchmark gap between Astra and Fable 5.1 already proved the leaderboard alone won’t tell you.
Key Takeaways
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared that “AGI has arrived” after OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra launch, but OpenAI itself never made that claim, and researchers call the term “jagged” rather than general.
- Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 post near identical scores on several benchmarks, yet produce noticeably different real world output. The gap traces back to the “harness” wrapped around the model, not the model itself.
- SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Cursor shows where the real competitive fight is moving. It’s not the raw model anymore. It’s who controls the layer around it.
AGI, artificial general intelligence, means a system that can match or beat human performance across essentially any cognitive task, not just the narrow ones it was trained for. That distinction matters because it’s exactly what’s being argued about right now.
Jensen Huang has a habit of declaring victory at the exact moment his company needs the market to believe it. So when OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra on Sept. 3, Huang posted on X that “AGI has arrived,” adding that “400K GPUs” are “coming online next.”
I’m an AI engineer, and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I spent the last year watching every model release get relabeled as the one that finally changes everything. Here is the truth.
results.summary:
OpenAI’s release of the GPT-6 Astra model has sparked debate over the arrival of artificial general intelligence, shifting industry focus toward the infrastructure surrounding these powerful AI systems.

### Key Points
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang claimed GPT-6 Astra signifies the arrival of AGI, though OpenAI has not officially adopted this terminology for the new model.
- Researchers describe current AI capabilities as "jagged," noting that systems often excel in specific domains while remaining unreliable in others.
- Benchmark scores for models like Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 can be misleading because performance depends heavily on the "harness" or infrastructure used.
- A harness—comprising prompt assembly, memory management, and tool access—can cause a single model's accuracy to swing by nearly 40 percentage points.
- SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Cursor highlights a strategic shift toward controlling the application layer rather than just the underlying AI models.

### Why it Matters
The industry is moving away from prioritizing raw model performance toward the infrastructure that enables practical, reliable AI workflows. Businesses should evaluate AI tools based on their specific operational harness and real-world reliability rather than relying on subjective AGI claims or standardized leaderboard scores.

results.title: LiteLLM Compromised in Fresh Supply Chain Attack
results.author: Ionut Arghire
results.content:
LiteLLM was compromised in a fresh supply chain attack, and malicious packages were served to its users on both PyPI and Docker.
The incident occurred on October 21 and involved version 1.107.0 of the popular open source proxy for routing requests across LLM providers.
The malicious packages were online for roughly three hours and are estimated to have been downloaded over 49,000 times. The packages were removed from PyPI, and Docker Hub tags and image variants were either removed or repointed to clean artifacts.
[Read: Trivy, Not LiteLLM Behind the 2,500 Org Compromise ]
Per LiteLLM’s investigation, the attackers obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens for “an unexpected, innocuously named user account in our internal LiteLLM deployment, which was exposed to the public internet”.
The tokens were likely leaked by Claude Code, which, in specific circumstances, would embed them into a response body, which may be logged to LiteLLM logs. The attackers likely retrieved the tokens from the logs.
However, it is still unclear how the attackers accessed the internal deployment or moved laterally, as they had access to three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials, LiteLLM says.
The attackers used the compromised credentials to disable branch protections, merge a change that pointed the releaser to a different source repository, and run a compromised GitHub workflow that pointed to a lookalike repository, then signed and published the poisoned artifacts.
Users who downloaded the malicious LiteLLM version 1.107.0 packages during the compromise window were infected with malware that serves as an information stealer and a RAT. According to LiteLLM, its enterprise customers pulling from its private repository were not affected.
Likely built with the help of AI and served from Berri-AI/litellm, which poses as the legitimate BerriAI/litellm repository, the payload extracts three files into the site-packages root to be executed whenever a Python interpreter runs.
First, the interpreter loads the stealer, which harvests system information, browser credentials and cookies, developer credentials, environment variables, cloud secrets (AWS, GCP, and Azure), AI tool API keys (Anthropic, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI, and more), SSH private keys, shell history files, and GPG keys.
The stolen data is encrypted and sent to litellm[.]dev.
Cybersecurity outfit Wiz says the attackers started abusing the stolen credentials roughly 4.5 hours after they were exfiltrated.
Wiz observed the attackers querying Amazon Bedrock models with stolen AWS credentials, suggesting LLMjacking.
The RAT component of the malware was observed regularly checking with the attackers’ command-and-control (C&C) server. It also “checks a GitHub dead drop every hour and runs whatever Python the attacker serves,” StepSecurity notes.
Users who installed LiteLLM version 1.107.0 should immediately remove it, rotate their credentials, and sweep their systems for malware. The most recent clean LiteLLM version is 1.106.2.
Related: AOMEI Backupper Compromised in Short-Burst Supply Chain Campaign
Related: Rank Math PRO WordPress Plugin Compromised in Supply Chain Attack
Related: $86 Million Crypto Heist Linked to Ledger Signer Hardware Implant
Related: Long-Running NPM Malware Campaign Accumulates 40,000 Downloads
results.summary:
LiteLLM suffered a supply chain attack on October 21, resulting in over 49,000 downloads of a malicious version containing information-stealing malware and remote access trojan capabilities.

### Key Points
- Attackers compromised LiteLLM version 1.107.0 by hijacking GitHub CLI OAuth tokens to publish poisoned packages to PyPI and Docker Hub.
- The malicious code remained active for approximately three hours before being removed, with enterprise customers using private repositories remaining unaffected.
- The malware harvests sensitive data, including cloud secrets, SSH keys, browser credentials, and API keys for AI services like OpenAI and Anthropic.
- Cybersecurity firm Wiz reported that attackers used stolen AWS credentials to perform LLMjacking by querying Amazon Bedrock models.
- Users who installed the compromised version are advised to immediately rotate all credentials and scan their systems for persistent malware.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant risks posed by supply chain attacks on open-source tools that manage sensitive developer credentials and cloud infrastructure. The compromise demonstrates how easily attackers can leverage leaked tokens to gain lateral access and exfiltrate high-value data from development environments.

results.title: U.S. warns of active Chinese cyber probes on power grids and water systems using AI-generated attack tools
results.author: Willow Tohi
results.content:
For the first time, U.S. intelligence agencies have confirmed that adversaries are actively scanning the nation's most sensitive industrial control systems using artificial intelligence to write custom exploitation code. On August 19, a joint advisory documented how state-sponsored actors are conducting reconnaissance against U.S.-based industrial installations using AI-generated scripts disguised as legitimate monitoring tools. The advisory specifically warns of actors with ties to a cybersecurity company providing infrastructure for botnets and network intrusions. The threat is focused across six critical infrastructure sectors, and the advisory notes this is not theoretical—it is an active, ongoing threat with actors currently probing infrastructure.
Traditional cyber intrusions required months of manual code writing by highly skilled programmers. That barrier has collapsed. According to the joint advisory, threat actors are using open-source industrial automation libraries—specifically snap7.dll and python-snap7—combined with AI-assisted scripting to create custom tools that mimic legitimate operational technology monitoring software. These tools provide read/write access to Siemens S7 Series PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic programs via the S7comm protocol.
The advisory warns that AI "dramatically reduces the technical expertise and time required to develop working ICS exploitation scripts and malicious tools." Adversaries can now use internet scanning services to find exposed PLCs running outdated software, then quickly deploy AI-generated scripts to exploit them. The potential consequences: disruption of critical industrial processes, safety incidents, equipment damage, data compromise and cascading failures across interconnected systems.
This advisory arrives amid a sobering historical pattern. The 2021 Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack demonstrated that a single digital intrusion could halt fuel delivery across the Eastern Seaboard. The 2015 Ukrainian power grid attack—widely attributed to Russian state actors—cut electricity to 225,000 customers. Today's threat is more systemic: Rather than targeting a single pipeline or substation, adversaries are positioning themselves within the programmable logic controllers that form the backbone of modern industrial civilization.
The NSA's August advisory explicitly calls this an "evolution in threat actor capabilities." The shift to AI-generated tools means the barrier to entry for attacking power plants, water treatment facilities and chemical processors has dropped precipitously. This is compounded by the October 8 warning naming Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI describes as a "key enabler" of malicious cyber activity with ties to the Chinese government, using large-scale botnets to target government, critical manufacturing and healthcare organizations worldwide.
Separate but concurrent threats compound the danger. The Gunra ransomware-as-a-service program, first appearing in 2025 and expanding to RaaS operations in 2026, now targets 16 sectors including healthcare, financial services, transportation, utilities and government. The FBI observed Gunra actors collecting business-critical documents, databases, personally identifiable information and internal email communications before deploying encryption.
Meanwhile, evolving threat intelligence suggests the Russian government "may be considering potential cyber attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure." While no incident is guaranteed, the convergence of Chinese state-sponsored AI-driven reconnaissance, Russian state interest and criminal ransomware operations creates an unprecedented threat environment. A comprehensive cyberattack halting power supply, transportation and hospital services could cause a crisis dwarfing the COVID-19 pandemic.
The advisory provides a clear playbook. Organizations must prioritize patching known exploited vulnerabilities, disable external management capabilities on internet-exposed PLCs, and implement offline, immutable backups that are regularly tested. Network segmentation between information technology and operational technology systems remains critical. The NSA urges organizations to "review this advisory to be aware of the wide range of tactics used by these actors and implement recommended actions and mitigations."
Key immediate steps recommended by the advisory:
The nation stands at a crossroads. The joint advisory is not a speculative warning—it documents active reconnaissance against the systems that power homes, treat drinking water and manufacture food. As one security analyst noted, "Even a little preparation can be helpful, just in case." The principle that critical infrastructure should be off-limits to attack must be supported by action. Responsible countries must take measures against cyber criminals operating within their borders. Experts from allied nations have agreed to work together on specific understandings regarding off-limit targets. Today's warnings, based on evolving threat intelligence, demand that every organization in the critical infrastructure sectors treat this as an operational priority. The crisis of a comprehensive cyber attack may not be guaranteed, but neither is the grace of avoiding one.

U.S. intelligence agencies have confirmed that state-sponsored adversaries are actively using artificial intelligence to develop custom code for scanning and exploiting sensitive industrial control systems across critical infrastructure.

### Key Points
- A joint August 19 advisory warns that state-sponsored actors are using AI to create scripts that mimic legitimate monitoring tools to probe industrial installations.
- Threat actors are leveraging open-source libraries like snap7.dll to gain unauthorized read/write access to Siemens S7 Series programmable logic controllers.
- The FBI has identified Integrity Technology Group as a key enabler of these activities, noting its ties to the Chinese government and use of large-scale botnets.
- Adversaries are targeting six critical infrastructure sectors, including power, water, and manufacturing, to potentially disrupt essential services and cause equipment damage.
- The NSA recommends that organizations immediately patch known vulnerabilities, disable external management for internet-exposed controllers, and implement strict network segmentation.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into cyber warfare significantly lowers the technical barrier for adversaries to disrupt the foundational systems that power modern society. This shift creates an unprecedented threat environment where critical infrastructure, such as power grids and water treatment facilities, faces a heightened risk of systemic failure.

results.title: The Stakes of Brazil’s Presidential Election
results.author: The Intercept Briefing
results.content:
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday in one of the most consequential presidential elections of the last decade. The run-off election will determine the future of the largest democracy in Latin America and the fate of the Amazon rainforest.
Incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing off against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The elder Bolsonaro is currently on house arrest for his role in a failed 2023 military coup that intended to assassinate Lula, his vice president, and a Supreme Court justice. Despite his father’s attempted coup, Flavio Bolsonaro is currently the frontrunner, after coming out slightly ahead in the first round of voting.
“If they don’t win this election, then not only is Jair going to stay in jail, most likely, but Eduardo, Flávio’s brother and Jair’s son, who is in self-exile in the U.S., he has a multiyear prison sentence for his actions in the U.S. lobbying against Brazil’s foreign interests. He’s not going to be able to go home if they lose this election,” says Andrew Fishman, a Rio de Janeiro-based investigative journalist. “So they’re really just willing to do whatever they can to make sure that they win because this is their only get-out-of-jail-free card.”
Sound familiar? This week on The Intercept Briefing, host Jessica Washington speaks with Fishman, president and co-founder of The Intercept Brasil, about what’s at stake for Brazil and the planet in Sunday’s election.
“It’s a global election. The voters in Brazil will be deciding the future of humanity,” Fishman tells The Intercept. Jair Bolsonaro oversaw significant deforestation of the Amazon rainforest, leaving the ecological and climate linchpin in danger of becoming a “savanna.” Now, he argues, his son can finish the job. “You’re going to have an international migration crisis,” says Fishman. “It’s really self-defeating because the cattle ranchers are his base. They are the ones that are wanting to do the things that will end their future profitability — the future existence of their business.”
President Donald Trump has taken a particular interest in the race, as he seeks to expand U.S. influence and control across the Western Hemisphere. “Brazil — as the biggest economy, the biggest country, the most powerful entity in the hemisphere besides the United States — if Brazil falls, then the rest falls in line,” says Fishman. “But if Brazil remains as this big island of resistance in the middle of the continent, it really messes up [the Trump administration’s] plans, doesn’t it?”
Big Tech is also looming large over the race. “There’s all these pieces of circumstantial evidence that suggest that Meta is interfering in this election, and they have every incentive to do so. They will have a much better regulatory environment if Flávio wins because of Flávio’s submissiveness to U.S. interests and his willingness to play ball with whatever Trump tells him to,” adds Fishman.
In a request for comment, Meta said, “Meta applies the same rules to every candidate, every party and every political viewpoint in Brazil, as we do in elections around the world. We do not suppress content to disadvantage one side, and we do not give preferential treatment to any side. Each of the incidents cited by Lula’s campaign has a straightforward, documented explanation. … Brazilian voters deserve facts, not a political narrative built by combining unrelated technical issues. Meta will continue to enforce its rules, comply with Brazilian electoral law, fix mistakes when they occur and provide a level playing field for everyone who uses our services.”
As U.S. leaders attempt to mold Brazil into a satellite state, Fishman argues the United States is slowly becoming more and more like its southern neighbor.
“It’s not that Brazil is becoming more like the United States, it’s that the United States is becoming more like Brazil,” says Fishman. “You have just shrinking spheres of democracy while oligarchs have increasing power and control and are able to do what they want and insist on decisions for the country that are bad for all of the society and the people, but good for their individual interests.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Jessica Washington: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing, I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter at The Intercept.
Akela Lacy: I’m Akela Lacy, senior politics reporter at The Intercept. Jessie, what do our listeners need to know about this week?
JW: I’ve been following a pretty disturbing story that’s actually centered on a campaign ad. Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy released what I would argue is the ugliest campaign ad of a dark season. That is, of course, a season of campaign ads filled with Islamophobic, transphobic, sexist rhetoric, and racist rhetoric as well. But in the ad, the mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton accuses her daughter of being a liar, claiming “she’s lied her whole life.”
Now, what makes this really dark is that Acton was removed from her mother’s care at 12 years old, after she alleges she was raped by her mother’s then-40-year-old husband.
AL: That’s horrible. Has Acton responded?
JW: Acton responded to the attack ad saying, “My brother Phil and I endured abuse, hunger, and neglect. We were often kept in a dark basement, were frequent-fliers with child protective services, and lived in fear of our birth mother’s violent and erratic temper. I’ve always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it’s sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain.”
This is one, as I’ve said, of the darkest campaign ads in a really horrifying season of campaign ads.
Akela, I know you’ve been tracking another big election story this week on a beat you’ve covered for a really long time, and that’s [American Israel Public Affairs Committee].
AL: So we have been covering extensively the way that AIPAC’s strategy has changed over the last few election cycles since they started spending directly on campaigns.
If you’ve been following our reporting, you know that we’ve written a lot about both their super PAC, United Democracy Project, and this shell PAC strategy where there were a number of different groups that popped up throughout the midterm season, took money from AIPAC, spent against candidates that AIPAC didn’t like, and then — per filings that came out this week — shut down and gave all their money back to AIPAC.
So the idea being that, they had been trying to shield what was an increasingly toxic reputation amid the ongoing genocide in Gaza from creating backlash against their activity in these races.
Jewish Insider scooped on Wednesday that AIPAC announced that it will no longer endorse candidates or give PAC contributions through its AIPAC PAC. Now, this doesn’t mean that they will stop spending on elections. Their super PAC, United Democracy Project, will continue to spend, as it has been pouring record amounts of money into various races. But this is getting a lot of attention, both from the left and I would say from the center.
The left, Justice Democrats in particular, and candidates who are no longer in Congress, but I saw Jamaal Bowman talking about this, saying that this is the culmination of the fight that the left has been putting up against AIPAC in elections. I don’t know that I would categorize this as a win necessarily, considering that the super PAC seems like it’s going to continue to spend a lot of money. But that was the big news in my campaign finance world this week.
JW: You’ve done a lot of really interesting coverage of how AIPAC is moving their money around through these different PACs and trying to get around the fact that people really dislike AIPAC, and that it has really tarnished the reputation of candidates who take this money. Obviously, this is a maneuver to get rid of the reputational harm of AIPAC money while still giving people AIPAC money.
I’ve actually been tracking a story completely off our election cycle, and that’s what’s going on in France. I know we touched on that a couple weeks ago but, really, these protests have taken on another life.
For those who don’t know, in France, there were these protests that were initially launched by students primarily in the suburbs concerned about educational inequality. This meant staffing shortages and poor facilities. But it has exploded into a nationwide uprising about the cost of living and broader economic inequality.
Now, perhaps unsurprisingly, and not to bring it too quickly back to the U.S., but President Donald Trump has used this as an opportunity to rail against immigrants. So despite the fact that there is zero indication any of the violence has been spurred on by immigrants. At a campaign rally on Monday, he told the crowd, “If Europe doesn’t close its borders and bring the criminals out, like the people that are protesting, Europe is finished.”
So yeah, that’s just one other example of how Donald Trump has inserted himself into international politics.
AL: Trump has also inserted himself into politics in a different region in the world. We have the Brazilian elections for president heading to a runoff this week. I know you spoke, Jessie, to Andrew Fishman, an investigative reporter and president and co-founder of The Intercept Brasil, about those elections.
JW: It’s a really interesting election with a ton of parallels to the political situation in the United States, as well as, as you’ve pointed out, a ton of influence from the United States. On Sunday, Brazil will have a run-off presidential election that will determine the future of not only Latin America’s largest democracy, but also — and this is really important — the fate of the Amazon rainforest, and one could argue, the planet.
This is the first presidential election since former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro was imprisoned on house arrest in an attempted military coup, a sentence that his son, the current frontrunner, Flávio Bolsonaro has promised to overturn.
I talked to Andrew about the media landscape, the history of military leadership, and the outside influences that have made this a tight race, despite the fact that the perceived frontrunner is running on freeing the man who attempted a coup years prior.
President Luiz Inácio Lula de Silva is running for reelection. He’s accused both President Donald Trump and Meta of attempting to sway the election in favor of Flávio Bolsonaro.
The Intercept reached out to Meta for comment, and Meta denied interfering in the election process, saying they do not suppress content to disadvantage one side or give preferential treatment to the other.
But this is a really interesting conversation with Andrew, and I’m excited for people to get to hear it.
AL: As am I. Let’s hear it.
JW: Andrew, welcome to The Intercept Briefing.
Andrew Fishman: Hi, thanks for having me.
JW: On Sunday, Brazilians will head to the polls in a runoff presidential election between right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, and incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to determine the leadership of Latin America’s largest democracy and biggest economy.
Now, this is the first presidential election since former President Jair Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed the Capitol in 2023 and attempted to overturn the election results. Now, Flávio Bolsonaro, his son and ally, is widely considered to be the frontrunner after coming out slightly ahead in the first round of voting.
But as of Tuesday, his lead in the polls has been narrowing. Andrew, big picture, what are the major issues at play in this election on Sunday?
AF: If you want to be really direct about it, it’s the future of humanity.
You have one candidate who’s been responsible for record reductions of deforestation in the Amazon; and you have another one who’s saying, let’s chop it all down, and farmers should be able to do whatever they want on their land.
And under his father’s leadership, deforestation in the Amazon soared, as in the other regions in the area. Scientists think that there’s a major tipping point that we could be on the cusp of, that if we were to reach that, the Amazon will turn into a savanna. There would be no going back from that.
If that were to happen, all of the rain in South America comes from the Amazon, basically. [That would affect] the cattle ranching that’s doing the deforestation, no more of the soy that’s doing the deforestation — people would have trouble feeding themselves. São Paulo would probably run out of water, which it has done in the past.
It’s very precarious. So you would be having mass refugee influxes, migrations. I really do think that this election is on that scale; it’s a global election. The voters in Brazil will be deciding the future of humanity, very possibly.
JW: To your point, his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro’s administration oversaw significant deforestation of the rainforest, which houses 10 percent of all [known] species on Earth, and his son appears to be moving in that same direction.
Flávio told reporters in August that he did not believe in climate change and that “the best way to address environmental issues is what we did during the Bolsonaro administration,” referring, of course, to the senior Bolsonaro’s administration.
What is at stake for climate change when we’re talking about this massive deforestation that could potentially be happening if Flávio wins?
AF: Every ecosystem in South America is interconnected and in the world. If the Amazon collapses and turns into savanna and the rainfall stops, and you have this massive drying out of the continent — which is one of the major exporters of food in the world — you’re going to have all of those issues locally, and that’s going to impact local markets and everything. You’re going to have an international migration crisis.
But on top of that, we have no idea what the ecological knock-on effects of that could be. With that, we could be having a more rapid increase in polar ice cap melting. With the temperatures increasing, it could be exacerbating the death of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current, which is the thing that would put Europe back into an ice age. It’s very possible that’s already happening right now.
We’re at this really tenuous moment for the climate, for the Earth, for humanity. And you have a candidate that says very proudly [he] doesn’t believe in any of that and wants to slash all mechanisms that are used to have more responsible management of land and prevent this massive catastrophe in just this proudly Luddite sort of way.
It’s really self-defeating because the cattle ranchers are his base. They are the ones that are wanting to do the things that will end their future profitability — the future existence of their business. It’s really self-defeating in this way for the Brazilians, and these very short-term benefits for massive long-term costs.
There’s estimates that the impact that the Amazon has for the global economy is in the hundreds of billions of dollars a year, and that benefit is far larger than the profits that they get out of these extractive industries that they do with farming and mining. It’s really hard to overstate the potential impacts that this could have.
JW: Is that urgency resonating with voters?
AF: Absolutely not. That is not what people are voting about, unfortunately. It’s what the people living in the heavy agricultural regions — where their local economy depends on that — they’re voting for Flávio for that reason. But the people who are voting against him, yes, there’s many people that care about the Amazon and want to preserve it, but it’s not the issue that’s being discussed day to day on TV, in the news, on the streets.
People are talking more about more human issues of corruption and who has better communication, security, economics. They’re not talking about the Amazon, unfortunately.
JW: That’s hardly surprising in the U.S. context, which I’m a little bit more acquainted with. Certainly climate, the environment, have never been top issues for voters, even if they’ve resonated more so with young people.
I did want to talk about another issue in the election, and that is the fate of Jair Bolsonaro. His son, Flávio Bolsonaro, has promised to free him. Jair Bolsonaro has been imprisoned on house arrest since 2025 for plotting a military coup. How is that particular campaign promise landing with the electorate in Brazil, and are you at all surprised by the public’s response?
AF: It’s very clear that for the Bolsonaros, this is an all-or-nothing for them. If they don’t win this election, then not only is Jair going to stay in jail, most likely, but Eduardo, Flávio’s brother and Jair’s son, who is in self-exile in the U.S., he has a multiyear prison sentence for his actions in the U.S. lobbying against Brazil’s foreign interests. He’s not going to be able to go home if they lose this election.
For them, it’s been very clear, and they’ve even said it in moments, that’s what this is about for them: their ability to get their father out of prison and to get themselves off the hook. Also, if you’re elected president, the investigations on things you did before you got elected, they go away.
So then Flávio’s off the hook, and he’s so wrapped up in so many different schemes and accusations and active investigations, some of which that we have revealed, including U.S. and abroad and offshore bank accounts and money laundering and potential connections to organized crime and militias. So they’re really just willing to do whatever they can to make sure that they win because this is their only get-out-of-jail-free card. To do that, they’re going to completely change the structure of the Supreme Court, and they’ll be able to put in a majority even without impeachment. They already have the Senate and the lower house of Congress.
They would control all of the executive branch. They have the majority of governorships that are in their coalition, and they run the local police. And the executive has control over the federal police and all the investigative and regulatory agencies. So they would have just absolute lockstep control over every branch of government federally and most of local government as well.
It would be a democratically elected coup.
JW: And voters, do they care about that? Do they care about the preservation of democracy? Is this ranking as a top election issue?
AF: It’s always double speak, right? Both sides say that they’re preserving democracy. The Bolsonaristas say that Lula and the Supreme Court are running a judicial dictatorship right now because they were getting censored and put in jail for actively plotting a coup, which included active planning to assassinate Lula after he was elected, his vice president after he was elected, and a member of the Supreme Court. So that’s what they’re [Jair Bolsonaro and military officials] in jail for. That’s why they were getting pushback, and they’re saying that having the pushback against that is a dictatorship.
In the meantime, you have the Lulistas who are saying that what the Bolsonaros want to do is a coup because they actively have said year after year, over and over again, “We want a coup. results.title: Your guide to voting in New York's 2026 elections for governor and Congress
results.author: Walter Wuthmann, Jon Campbell, Brigid Bergin
results.content:
Election Day is Nov. 3, and it’s time to choose New York’s next governor, attorney general, and congressmembers.
Will voters give Gov. Kathy Hochul a second full term in office? Or will they replace her with Bruce Blakeman, the Republican Nassau County executive with close ties to President Donald Trump? Will Attorney General Letitia James retain her role as the state’s top law enforcement official? And how will New York City voters decide on a series of ballot questions championed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani?
As you wait in line to cast your ballot, here’s a rundown of the candidates, ballot questions and other information.
How and when to vote in NYC
If you want to vote in person, you can find your polling site at vote.nyc.
But you’ll need to remember these key dates:
Oct. 24: In-person early voting begins. Find your early polling site here. Note that hours differ by day, so check the schedule before you go vote. This is also the last day for new voter registration, either online or in-person at your poll site.
Nov. 1: Early voting ends.
Nov. 2: Last day to apply in-person for a mail or absentee ballot at your county’s Board of Elections office.
Nov. 3: Election Day. Polls are open 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. Find your polling site here. (It’s likely different from your early-voting site). Mail-in ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 3.
New York’s candidates for governor
Kathy Hochul, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Universal childcare and building more housing. Enacted a moratorium on large data centers. Sent utility rebate checks of up to $200.
Resume: Became the state’s first female governor in 2021 after Andrew Cuomo's resignation. Previously served as lieutenant governor, U.S. representative and Erie County clerk.
Quote: “ Your family is my fight.”
Bruce Blakeman, Republican
Policy priorities: Cutting income taxes and lowering utility bills. Opposes sanctuary policies that restrict the state’s cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Opposes data center moratorium.
Resume: First elected Nassau County executive in 2021. Previously served as Hempstead town councilmember and Port Authority commissioner.
Quote: “We can’t afford four more years of Kathy Hochul.”
New York’s candidates for attorney general
Letitia James, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Crackdown on illegal firearms and ghost guns, protecting immigrants’ legal rights, and going after predatory lenders and mortgage providers. Has sued the Trump administration over 50 times.
Resume: Attorney general since 2019. Previously served as New York City's public advocate, making her the first Black woman to win and hold citywide office, and a New York City Councilmember representing parts of Brooklyn.
Quote: “No one is above the law, not even the President.”
Saritha Komatireddy, Republican
Policy priorities: More prosecution of street crime, like shoplifting and drug trafficking. Audit and investigate homeless shelters. Investigate waste, fraud and abuse in the public and private sectors.
Resume: Former assistant U.S. attorney in Brooklyn, where she helped prosecute leaders of Al-Qaeda, Islamic State, and Mexican drug cartels. Former chief of staff of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration under the Biden administration.
Quote: “Public safety is not optional. It’s time for accountability, action and real change.”
New York’s candidates for state comptroller
Tom DiNapoli, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Transition fund investments to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. Audit every school district in the state on a rotating cycle. Grew the pension fund to its historic high of $291 billion.
Resume: Second longest-serving comptroller in state history, first elected to the position in 2007. Former state assemblymember representing Nassau County.
Quote: “Transparency is essential so New Yorkers can hold their government and elected officials accountable.”
Joseph Hernandez, Republican
Policy priorities: Aggressively audit state agencies, public authorities and programs. Review state contracts. Create a $10 billion “Empire Opportunity Fund” to invest in emerging businesses and industries, similar to a sovereign wealth fund.
Resume: Longtime Wall Street investor, currently the founder and senior managing partner of Blue Water Venture Partners. Cuban refugee who fled the country at age 7.
Quote: “The fraud and abuse in New York is out of control.”
NYC ballot questions
Voters will find five questions on the back of their ballot. You can read our full breakdown of every question here.
The commission that wrote the proposals says they would:
- Streamline the approval process for pedestrian ramps, benches and sidewalk cafés.
- Modernize city contracting to expand opportunities for small businesses and nonprofit organizations.
- Accelerate road safety projects and the activation of underutilized city property.
- Simplify the building permitting process.
- Require contributions to the rainy day fund to strengthen long-term fiscal resilience.
Congressional races
17th District, Northern Westchester County and the Hudson Valley
Mike Lawler, Republican (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Led battle to expand the state and local tax deduction. Opposes sanctuary policies. Supports reopening Indian Point nuclear plant.
Resume: First elected to the House in 2022. Previously served in the state Assembly.
Quote: “ I'm proud of the fact that I've been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress.”
Cait Conley, Democrat
Policy priorities: Supports a public option for health insurance, banning congressmembers from trading stocks and creating a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants living in the United States.
Resume: Former director for counterterrorism on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden. Army officer who served in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Quote: “You deserve better. You deserve a patriot, not a puppet.”
3rd District, Northeast Queens and parts of Nassau and Suffolk counties
Tom Suozzi, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Opposes Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran. Supports an all-of-the-above approach to energy production, including green energy, natural gas and nuclear.
Resume: First elected to Congress in 2016. Retired to run for governor in 2022, lost the primary to Gov. Kathy Hochul. Re-elected to his old seat in 2024 after Congress expelled Rep. George Santos.
Quote: “I will fight for you against the extremists.”
Mike LiPetri, Republican
Policy priorities: Supports deporting undocumented immigrants with criminal records. Opposes boycotts of Israel and regulations on cryptocurrency.
Resume: Served in the state Assembly from 2019-2021. Ran for this seat in 2024 and lost to Suozzi.
Quote: “I stood up to the radical left agenda that threatened our quality of life and drove up our cost of living.”
4th District, Nassau County
Laura Gillen, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Supports eliminating the cap on the state and local tax deduction, and extending temporary protected status for Haitians living in the United States. Opposes cuts to Medicaid.
Resume: First elected to the seat in 2024. Former town supervisor of Hempstead.
Quote: “My number one priority is representing Long Islanders, not Trump.”
Jeanine Driscoll, Republican
Policy priorities: Supports restoring the full state and local tax deduction and strengthening the United States' border with Mexico.
Resume: Town of Hempstead receiver of taxes, first elected in 2019.
Quote: “There’s a lot of middle-class people in the district who need relief that’s not being offered to them right now through the current representation.”
1st District, Suffolk County
Nick LaLota, Republican (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Supports deporting undocumented immigrants with criminal records and tax cuts. Opposes offshore drilling on Long Island.
Resume: First elected to Congress in 2022. Served three deployments overseas as a naval officer.
Quote: “My mission is simple: to make Suffolk safer and more affordable for every family that calls this amazing place home.”
Christopher Gallant, Democrat
Policy priorities: Supports developing more housing near transit stations, refinancing federal student loans, and expanding child tax credits.
Resume: Former Army pilot and air traffic controller local union president.
Quote: “I’m not running to make noise. I’m running to do the work.”
11th District, Staten Island and South Brooklyn
Nicole Malliotakis, Republican (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Increase funding for the Department of Homeland Security and ICE. Suspend the federal gas tax to reduce energy costs.
Resume: First elected to the House in 2020. Previously served in the state Assembly.
Quote: “I said I was going to fight to secure our border and deport criminals from our streets and that’s exactly what we did.”
Mike DeCillis, Democrat
Policy priorities: Raise the corporate tax rate and create a single-payer healthcare system.
Resume: Former first responder, NYPD officer and special education teacher.
Quote: “I know that everyone in the district deserves to have their voice heard in government, and that they are currently not.”

results.title: Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
Britain cannot let aritificial intelligence be ruled by "tech bros and oligarchs", the AI minister has said.
Kanishka Narayan told the BBC's Political Thinking podcast that dealing with the technology requires not only regulation, but "building capability and capacity in the state" too.
He compared AI to the Victorian-era Industrial Revolution, but said the country needed to transition better than it did back then.
His comments were recorded the day before Barclays banking group announced it was cutting 5,000 jobs in an AI-led efficiency drive.
He was also speaking before another major AI-related development - the discovery of a cyber-security flaw affecting millions of websites, which was found with the help of AI.
Narayan, who became the UK's first cabinet minister for AI when he was appointed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July, said the scale of the technological change was "something that we haven't seen for decades and decades".
"It is comparable and in some ways exceeds the Industrial Revolution," he said, referencing the shift from a predominantly agricultural economy to industrial and manufacturing sectors between about 1750 and 1900.
The Labour MP told the BBC's Nick Robinson that Britain needed to avoid what happened in the Industrial Revolution where "the outcome as a whole was good for the country, but the transition was extremely painful for too many people".
"The fundamental thing is that the British public and democracy has to assert power rather than leave it to tech bros and oligarchs," he added.
He did not name any specific companies or tech bosses.
As well as "pulling the lever of regulation", the country needs to build AI in Britain "so you can shape the working conditions" and avoid it all being developed abroad, he said.
"We need to build technology to defend ourselves and to grow ourselves so we have leverage internationally - we're now currently totally reliant on other countries for essential bits of technology," he added.
Pointing to the capabilities of AI, he said the government recently used frontier AI models, external in Whitehall to check for cybersecurity issues.
"We only spent £13,000 on it - we discovered 500 new vulnerabilities. These are novel vulnerabilities that we discovered in significant areas of the public sector," Narayan said, without detailing what they were.
He also said his conversations with Chancellor John Healey had hinted at a potential AI announcement in next week's Budget, though he did not say what this was.
Narayan rejected the notion that the US and China were the only powers that matter for AI, saying the UK's AI Security Institute had seen "every US lab...coming to us" asking it to test models before deployment.
Earlier this month, Narayan warned it was likely the UK's cyber defences will at some point be breached, after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June.
He has made a series of interventions in recent weeks after an AI safety researcher went public with claims that people building the technology believed it could destroy humanity.
results.summary:
UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan has warned that the government must assert democratic control over artificial intelligence to prevent the technology from being dominated by private tech interests.

### Key Points
- Kanishka Narayan, the UK's first cabinet minister for AI, stated that the nation must build domestic technological capacity rather than relying solely on foreign-developed systems.
- The minister compared the current AI shift to the Industrial Revolution, emphasizing the need to manage the transition to avoid widespread social and economic hardship.
- Government officials recently utilized frontier AI models to identify 500 novel cybersecurity vulnerabilities within the public sector at a cost of £13,000.
- Narayan highlighted the UK's influence in AI safety, noting that major US laboratories are seeking testing services from the British AI Security Institute.
- The comments follow Barclays' recent announcement of 5,000 job cuts driven by an AI-led efficiency strategy.

### Why it Matters
This policy shift signals a move toward greater state intervention in the development and deployment of emerging technologies to protect national security and labor markets. By prioritizing domestic capability, the government aims to reduce reliance on international tech giants and ensure that AI integration does not destabilize the broader economy.

results.title: Xbox hijacks your custom background for Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 ads
results.author: jez@windowscentral.com (Jez Corden) , Jez Corden
results.content:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 looks set to be the best Call of Duty this decade thus far, but I'd give this marketing stunt a 0/10.
Ads are annoying at the best of times. If you're reading Windows Central without an adblocker (thanks!), you're probably getting bombarded in all directions by ads right now (sorry. But also, no, us lowly writers have no control over that). But hey, they keep the lights on, and Windows Central is free without paywalls at least, right?
You know what isn't free? Your shiny Xbox Series X|S console. That wasn't free. You know what else isn't free? Xbox Game Pass, nor is Xbox Game Pass Ultimate. Nor is Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, in fact. And today, even if you already purchased the game, Xbox is making sure that your console has a very yellow theme this morning — whether you like it or not.
I get that Call of Duty is incredibly important to Xbox's bottom line these days, and funds from the franchise are effectively propping up a variety of other bets Xbox is making right now. I get that last year's "disappointing" Call of Duty pulled down Xbox's financials overall, heaping on additional pressure for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to deliver.
Reviews suggest that Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 absolutely has delivered, by the way, with what fans and critics have been calling the best campaign maybe in a decade. It even has the top spot in sales on both Xbox and PlayStation as of writing, beating out GTA 6 itself (for now).
Does it really really need to take over my entire Xbox dashboard, though?
Today, Xbox fans woke up and noticed that Call of Duty not only has the entire spread of those loathed advertising tiles across the bottom of the dash, but also usurps your custom background. I went over to the Personalization settings and no, changing the background doesn't fix it.
You can actually disable this, however, (thanks Donkeyz) using the following steps.
How to turn off full-screen background ads on the Xbox Series X|S dashboard
- Open Settings via the Xbox guide menu.
- Navigate to General.
- Open Personalization.
- Go to My backgrounds. You might have to enter your pin.
- Disable "Show event-themed backgrounds."
Xbox's ads have long been a source of irritation. Sometimes they can be useful, helping discover new games (rarely, I might add), or deals and in-game events you might've missed. This, though? It's too much, IMO.
At least when Xbox was doing those full-screen pop-ups on boot, you could peruse and then dismiss at your leisure. It's not a big deal ultimately, you're not really on the dashboard for any length of time if you're just passing through to get to a game ... but it initially struck me as another annoying hint we don't actually own the shit we buy.
Big tech is aggressively fighting ownership
There seems to be a wider theme at play here. Yes it's just a temporary picture that will probably be gone by the end of the day, and yes you can disable it (for now ...) but it continues a trend of companies like Microsoft reminding us that we don't actually own or control the stuff we buy from them. Windows 11 itself has been blasted for the abundance of "recommended content" it comes with out of the box, and most don't know how to turn some of it off, or that they even can.
PlayStation has triggered a huge backlash over the summer by ending support for physical discs, with figures testifying in court that purchasing games grants you a license only — something many of us already knew, but they're increasingly testing the definition of this in recent years.
RELATED: How to turn off Windows 11 tracking and ads
Digital rights and even physical rights have been increasingly called into question in recent years. Whether it's companies like John Deere fighting against farmers' rights to repair their tractors, companies like BMW or Tesla charging a subscription to turn on features that already exists in your cars. What about companies like Apple intentionally making their laptops impossible to fix without specialist tools (offered by them only)? Companies are really really fighting against your right to actually own the things you buy from them.
Which comes back to the Xbox dashboard. Yes it's just a background today, no big deal right? But what happens tomorrow? Will Microsoft starting putting dashboard customization in as a premium feature? Microsoft is already charging playtime by the hour in Xbox Cloud Gaming ... is that the future of "ownership"? OpenAI's Sam Altman has been fully mask off with hopes that compute in general will be a rented accommodation in the future.
The Xbox Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 dashboard take over is irritating and inconvenient, and an pretty shameless reminder that Xbox can hijack your console whenever it feels like it, even if you paid the full recent $799 price tag ...
Am I paranoid? Maybe ... but maybe you're not paranoid ENOUGH! ... maybe.

Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea. Follow on X.com/JezCorden and tune in to the XB2 Podcast, all about, you guessed it, Xbox!

results.title: Attacks on Tech Firms Behind Most Third-Party Data Breach Victims
results.author: James Coker
results.content:
More than two-thirds (69%) of data breach victims in the past year were affected by a third-party breach, a new report by financial and risk advisory provider Kroll has found.
Of those individuals, most (79%) had their data accessed following the compromise of a technology company during the period June 2025 to June 2026.
This is far higher than the proportion of third-party data breaches emanating from other industries, which includes finance (9%), insurance (6%) or healthcare (5%).
Incidents affecting technology firms also caused 60% of the total number of data breach victims – whether emanating from a single organization or as part of a supply chain breach – over the 12-month period. This was followed by insurance (10%), finance (8%), healthcare (8%) and education (7.5%).
Among all security leaders surveyed for the Kroll report, published on October 22, 69% said their organization had suffered a breach in the previous 12 months, while 34% reported experiencing more than one.
Finance and Professional Services Most Breached Sectors
Despite the tech sector causing the vast majority of individual data breach victims, it was only the seventh most commonly breached sector.
In first place was finance, making up 20% of breaches observed by Kroll. This was followed by professional services (20%), healthcare (15%) and retail (8%).
In contrast, technology only made up 6% of data breach incidents.
The researchers said the discrepancy shows that despite an industry seeming more susceptible to breach, such as finance or healthcare, the domino effect of a company breach in the technology sector could be much more extensive.
Denyl Green, global head of breach notification at Kroll, commented, "Across most of the major incidents we handled over the past year, a vendor, software supplier or service provider was the link between the initial breach and the organizations affected. One incident can reach businesses and individuals who have never dealt directly with the company where the compromise began."
Cybercriminal actors such as the Scattered Spider hacking collective are known to target IT service providers to gain access to their customers’ systems.
In October 2026, it was reported that a Chinese nation-state actor gained access to IT management software provider ConnectWise’s cloud infrastructure, enabling the group to target downstream customers.
results.summary:
A new Kroll report reveals that 69% of data breach victims were impacted by third-party incidents, with technology companies serving as the primary source of these widespread compromises.

### Key Points
- Technology firms accounted for 79% of third-party data breaches between June 2025 and June 2026.
- Finance and professional services were the most frequently breached sectors, each representing 20% of total incidents.
- While technology companies caused 60% of all victim cases, they represented only 6% of total breach incidents.
- 69% of surveyed security leaders reported at least one organizational breach within the past 12 months.
- Cybercriminal groups, including the Scattered Spider collective, frequently target IT service providers to access downstream customer systems.

### Why it Matters
The data highlights a significant supply chain risk where a single compromise at a technology vendor can trigger a domino effect across multiple industries. Organizations must now prioritize third-party risk management to protect their data from vulnerabilities inherent in their software and service provider ecosystems.

results.title: Unvetted AI Agents Are Accessing US Bank Accounts
results.author: BeauHD
results.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Axios: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios. The difficulty in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot is forcing banks to block the technology and rapidly rewrite their terms of service. [...] This presents significant security risks: banking executives fear the steps agents with login access might take, especially if a user has granted purchase authority or the ability to shift funds. In other instances, some banks have tracked activity when agents -- programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf -- contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions, the people said.
Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances. The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents from accessing its platforms, sources familiar with the decision said. JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are also restricting agents. [...] Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said.
[...] On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure. But money isn't necessarily enough to solve this problem, one source said, because of how quickly the technology is developing and revealing new weaknesses in real time. Banks are investing in preventing worst-case scenarios, but they are also preparing for when those could happen, including with "day after" scenario planning that would allow them to quickly secure or restore customer access, sources said.
results.summary:
Major U.S. banks including JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Morgan Stanley are restricting third-party AI agents from customer accounts due to unauthorized activity and significant security concerns.

### Key Points
- Major financial institutions are blocking third-party AI agents that perform actions independent of user instructions.
- Banks struggle to distinguish between human users and automated bots, prompting updates to terms of service.
- Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi have implemented restrictions to prevent potential unauthorized financial transactions.
- Executives fear that AI agents with login credentials could shift funds or make purchases without explicit user authorization.
- Financial firms are conducting "day after" scenario planning to prepare for potential security breaches and system vulnerabilities.

### Why it Matters
The rise of autonomous AI agents creates a new security frontier that threatens the integrity of digital banking infrastructure. If banks cannot effectively verify user intent, they may be forced to permanently restrict third-party financial tools to protect customer assets and maintain regulatory compliance.

results.title: U-KNOCK 2026 Brings Korean Content Companies To Hollywood For Investment & Global Partnerships
results.author: Dianalodderhose
results.content:
U-KNOCK 2026 will connect Korean content and technology companies with U.S. investors and entertainment partners on November 4–6, 2026, at The Biltmore Los Angeles. The program is hosted by South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and organized by the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA).
Now in its third year, U-KNOCK builds on relationships with international investors and Hollywood studios, emphasizing deal-making and long-term partnerships. Key programs include the International Content Investment Forum on November 5 and one-on-one investment and business meetings on November 6.
The November 5 forum, themed “What Makes Content Last,” will bring together Korean and U.S. leaders in media, finance and technology to examine how cultural success becomes enduring commercial value. Discussions will explore IP monetization, global franchise expansion and emerging business models driven by AI, digital platforms and evolving investment strategies.
U.S. participants include The Raine Group; Shamrock Capital; Atwater Capital; J.P. Morgan Global Corporate Bank; Amblin Entertainment; and Anonymous Content, who all bring perspectives across entertainment finance, investment and production.
From Korea, speakers will include global transmedia company CJ ENM; YLAB, which develops webtoon universes and screen adaptations; character-IP company IPX (formerly LINE FRIENDS); creator-focused comedy label MetaComedy; Moneygraphy, the original-content media outlet from financial platform Toss; and bemyfriends, a provider of direct-to-consumer fandom business solutions. Together, they will examine how stories travel across formats, how content models evolve and how global fan communities can support sustainable businesses.
Five Korean companies will then present at the Korean Company Showcase. Modhaus, the company behind K-pop group tripleS and Web3 fan-participation platform COSMO, will appear alongside YN Culture & Space (YN C&S), known for its LED-wall virtual production and advanced production infrastructure; Klleon, which develops real-time multilingual interactive digital humans; Contents First, operator of Tappytoon and its global audience of more than 14 million readers; and Studio Eon, which uses an Unreal Engine-based pipeline to produce science-fiction animation. The companies will present their business models and plans for North American expansion.
On November 6, the five showcase participants will be joined by seven more companies for one-on-one business meetings. The full 12-company delegation spans original story IP in drama, film, animation and web novels, as well as generative AI, interactive entertainment and fan platforms. Meetings are intended to connect the companies with North American investors, buyers, studios and other potential business partners.
The additional participants include Big Ocean ENM, with crime procedurals Flex X Cop and Another Heaven, the latter in development; EO Content Group, developing action-espionage series TEAM-K; and Mstoryhub, whose webtoon IP includes The Remarried Empress. LOCUS is developing Kkokdu, a 3D family fantasy feature inspired by Korean funeral traditions. RECOV combines K-pop touring, merchandise and VIP services, while JIRO brings AI content-production platform Dropshot AI and AI-generated K-pop idol IP SEORIA. Draftify’s PlaySquad rounds out the lineup with playable livestreaming that lets viewers influence gameplay.
U.S. and international investors, buyers and production executives interested in attending the International Content Investment Forum or requesting one-on-one meetings with the 12 participating Korean companies can register and submit meeting requests at www.uknockglobal.com.

The U-KNOCK 2026 event will bring South Korean content and technology firms to The Biltmore Los Angeles from November 4–6 to foster partnerships with U.S. investors.

- The Korea Creative Content Agency is hosting the three-day event to facilitate deal-making between Korean media companies and Hollywood studios.
