This event serves as a strategic bridge for Korean media companies seeking to monetize intellectual property and secure capital within the competitive U.S. entertainment market. By connecting local creators with major financial institutions and production studios, the program aims to transform cultural content into sustainable, long-term global franchises.

results.title: Elon Musk's power now extends far beyond Tesla, and Ukraine shows why
results.author: Jake Conley
results.content:
How Elon Musk went from Tesla CEO to the 'most powerful civilian, non-governmental actor in history'
Elon Musk's influence over first Tesla (TSLA) and now SpaceX (SPCX) has long been measured in terms of corporate valuations, technological breakthroughs, and personal wealth, where his companies have made him the richest person in the world. Across the last few years, however, the centi-billionaire's growing portfolio of businesses has pushed him into a new lane entirely.
Over the past decade, Elon Musk has become far more than a corporate executive or political power broker. Through his control of companies underpinning global communications, military operations, space access, and artificial intelligence, Musk has acquired a degree of influence over national security, international relations, and the global economy that few private individuals have ever possessed.
"There's a very real chance that [Musk] is the most powerful civilian, non-governmental actor in history," Gautam Mukunda, a research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School and managing director of the consultancy Two Rivers Group, told Yahoo Finance. Musk "has resources that are vastly larger than those of all but a handful of governments on the planet."
That influence came into sharp focus this month when widely reported restrictions on SpaceX's satellite communications services disrupted Ukraine's military operations, exposing just how dependent a sovereign nation's battlefield capabilities had become on infrastructure supplied by a private-sector company.
There are conflicting accounts of who ordered the restrictions in Ukraine, which disrupted battlefield drones and prompted several hours of faltering drone speeds and faulty communications on the front lines of the nation's conflict with Russia. Musk says the White House controls Ukraine's access to Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, while officials in the Trump administration have said they weren't involved in the decision.
Regardless of responsibility, the incident has highlighted the increasing separation between corporate access to governments and governmental reliance on the private sector, particularly given Musk's singular control over rocketry and satellite communications.
'Extraordinary power'
SpaceX is now responsible for roughly 90% of all mass sent into orbit off Earth, Musk said on SpaceX's recent earnings call. The Pentagon is Starshield's largest customer, while countries such as the Philippines, Argentina, and Indonesia use Starlink for national communications, including emergency services.
"He can turn a country's communications on or off — that's an extraordinary power," Darrell West, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center for Technology Innovation, told Yahoo Finance. "Even governments can't do that."
results.summary:
Elon Musk has emerged as a uniquely powerful non-governmental actor, wielding significant influence over global communications, military operations, and space access through his leadership of Tesla and SpaceX.

### Key Points
- SpaceX currently manages approximately 90% of all mass launched into Earth's orbit, establishing Musk as a dominant force in global space infrastructure.
- The Pentagon serves as the primary customer for Starshield, a military-grade satellite communications network developed by SpaceX for national security applications.
- Recent disruptions to Starlink services in Ukraine highlighted the growing reliance of sovereign nations on private-sector technology for critical battlefield communications and drone operations.
- Countries including the Philippines, Argentina, and Indonesia utilize Starlink technology to support national communications and emergency service infrastructure.
- Experts from the Harvard Kennedy School and the Brookings Institution suggest Musk’s resources and control over essential technology exceed those of many sovereign governments.

### Why it Matters
The concentration of such critical infrastructure under a single private individual creates unprecedented challenges for international relations and national security. This shift forces governments to navigate a new reality where private corporate decisions can directly impact the success of military operations and global connectivity.

results.title: What OPT Is and How It Affects the Economy in 6 Charts
results.author: Johanna Alonso
results.content:
Photo illustration by Inside Higher Ed | seb_ra/iStock/Getty Images
The Trump administration’s proposed rule to charge colleges as much as $100,000 for their international students to participate in a temporary work program after graduation won’t just impact those students, experts argue.
A growing body of research into the impacts of highly skilled immigration on the American economy shows that international workers like those using optical practical training tend to spark innovation, build businesses and create new jobs—benefits that would be harder to realize if the OPT fee goes into effect.
“There is definitely a mentality and a belief among a lot of people that every student who works on OPT is literally taking a job from an American worker, and the thing that’s borne out of the economic literature is not so much that,” said Violet Buxton-Walsh, an immigration fellow with the Institute for Progress, a think tank focused on innovation. “It’s much more that OPT graduates are complements, not substitutes, to American workers.”
The fee is not yet final; the rule was proposed by the Department of Homeland Security earlier this month and is currently accepting public comments. A similar fee for H-1B was struck down by a judge.
Experts warn that the proposed fee would severely handicap—if not outright eradicate—the OPT program, which was formalized in 1992 under the George H.W. Bush administration, further expanded in 2008 and expanded once more in 2016, with the goal of bringing top global talent to the U.S. In recent years, the program has come under fire from conservatives for supposedly taking jobs away from Americans and opening the doors for international students to stay in the U.S. through fraudulent employment schemes.
But the program has become a key driver to bring international students to the United States. Advocates for international students worry that the fee, compounded with the administration’s other restrictions on international students, could lead to even steeper declines in their enrollment.
Unlike other visa programs, the government does not publish comprehensive data about OPT, so much of the research that exists uses proxies or focuses on high-skilled immigration broadly. Some organizations have also obtained more detailed information from colleges and surveys. The IFP is home to a large open-source repository of OPT records, which the organization received via a public records requests covering 16 years of data. Still, even that data was spotty, Buxton-Walsh said.
Despite those hiccups, the body of research that does exist shows how the program contributes to the U.S. economy and hints at how impactful limiting it could be.
The number of international students working on OPT has never been higher, according to data from the Institute of International Education, a nonprofit that facilitates international exchange programs. Since the 2015–16 academic year, the number of individuals on OPT has nearly doubled from roughly 147,000 to about 294,000. OPT participants also make up about a quarter of all F-1 visa holders in the U.S., compared to 15.4 percent a decade ago.
Most of that growth has been among graduates of master’s programs, according to OPT Observatory, IFP’s repository of data. That tracks with overall international student numbers, as the highest proportion of F-1 students are master’s students.
The growing number of students opting in to OPT also indicates that the program is becoming increasingly popular. In surveys, international students frequently report that OPT is a key reason they wanted to study in the U.S. and that they would be less likely to come to the U.S. without it.
For international students hoping to get their foot in the door at U.S. companies, the program can be a strong draw.
Another survey by Interstride, a college and career software technology for international students, found that the top reason international students said they wanted to come to the U.S. was because of the job opportunities available.
Sam Peak, policy manager for labor and mobility at the Economic Innovation Group, a policy think tank, said that OPT serves as something of a “trial run” for students to showcase their abilities to employers and potentially be sponsored for a H-1B visa, which allows companies to hire international workers in specialty roles. For students interested in staying in the country, he said, it can be a helpful tool.
“I would describe it as the starting point for how the United States attracts top international global talents,” he said. “It’s the mechanism that allows international students who have been accepted to study at a university to try their hand in the labor markets, gain experience, build up their networks and showcase their potential to employers.”
Because OPT has such a strong influence on international students, higher education leaders and experts also worry that the OPT fee could negatively affect university enrollment and institutional revenue.
How OPT Pays Off
OPT critics often raise concerns that participants are taking jobs that American workers could otherwise hold. But researchers say that fear is based on misunderstandings of the labor market.
Michael Clemens, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins University, is currently finishing research on STEM OPT workers’ impact on innovation in the cities where they work. His findings indicate that the presence of those workers leads to the creation of new jobs and businesses. It also fuels new patents, from both STEM OPT workers themselves and U.S. natives, spurred by collaboration with their colleagues on OPT. Those figures apply to students who are on OPT and when they continue working in the U.S. after completing their OPT, if they do.
“That’s a large economic stimulus,” Clemens said. “And when a city becomes a hub of innovation and entrepreneurship, that means more jobs for childcare workers and security workers and delivery workers and construction workers, and it ripples through the whole economy.”
Other research shows that demand for American workers actually increased in areas where OPT participants settled, possibly because those OPT workers created new companies—though the study did find a decrease in American workers who were recent graduates of master’s programs.
A significant number of OPT workers stay near their university after graduating, bolstering and filling high-demand positions within the communities that educated them, said Buxton-Walsh, who cataloged the OPT data collected by IFP. In 13 states, over half of all OPT participants who graduated from a university in that state continued to work at least one job in the same state.
“This pipeline is unusually important to some of those smaller, rural communities,” she said.
In an analysis of OPT Observatory data, Chris Glass, professor of the practice in the Lynch School of Education and Human Development at Boston College, argued that the program is not the “Big Tech subsidy,” as some critics claim. In a blog post, he wrote that 2022 data shows that 88 percent of placements were outside the top 100 companies. The median employer of OPT participants, he wrote, hires just three graduates.
“The employer backbone of OPT is real and distributed,” he wrote.
Researchers at the Economic Innovation Group also investigated what jobs OPT workers take, finding that they’re not all positions that Americans would likely occupy. For one, significant numbers of OPT participants work in fields that the federal government has deemed high demand, including artificial intelligence. They also earn more than domestic workers—bucking perceptions that foreign workers accept low pay, which gives them a cost advantage over their American counterparts; just weeks ago, Vice President JD Vance accused companies of replacing American employees with “foreign indentured servants.”
Peak, at EIG, noted that the unemployment rate for STEM graduates has historically been low even while participation in STEM OPT was increasing, indicating that OPT users are not taking jobs. And though many STEM graduates do not work in STEM fields, the researchers noted that that might not necessarily mean they failed to get the job they were seeking.
“It’s kind of a funny example, but Pope Leo—he has a STEM degree, too, and we don’t consider Pope Leo a failure,” said Peak. “We wouldn’t consider somebody who is a computer science major who is doing supply chain management a failure … Americans have more choice to be in these non-STEM roles, and it’s not necessarily evidence of overcrowding or lowering wages.”
results.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a new $100,000 fee for colleges to enroll international students in the Optional Practical Training work program after their graduation.

### Key Points
- The proposed rule aims to charge institutions up to $100,000 for international students participating in the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program.
- OPT participation has nearly doubled since the 2015–16 academic year, reaching approximately 294,000 individuals.
- Research suggests OPT participants act as economic complements to American workers, often fueling innovation, patent creation, and new business development.
- Data indicates that 88 percent of OPT placements occur outside of the top 100 largest companies, supporting a distributed network of employers.
- The program serves as a critical recruitment tool for U.S. universities, as many international students cite work opportunities as a primary reason for enrollment.

### Why it Matters
The proposed fee could significantly reduce international student enrollment, potentially threatening the financial stability of U.S. universities that rely on these students. Furthermore, experts warn that restricting the program may stifle regional economic growth and innovation by limiting the pipeline of high-skilled talent available to American employers.

results.title: Bitcoin, gold trim early losses as yen gives up gains. Oil stays near $100
results.author: Omkar Godbole
results.content:
Bitcoin, gold trim early losses as yen gives up gains. Oil stays near $100
Bitcoin and gold pared early losses as the yen gave up gains and Asian stocks rebounded, though oil near $100 keeps inflation risks in focus.
- Bitcoin recovered to nearly $82,000 during Asian trading Friday as gold, Asian stocks and Nasdaq futures rebounded while the Japanese yen surrendered early gains.
- About $435 million in cryptocurrency futures positions were liquidated over 24 hours, including $385 million in bullish bets, as bitcoin tested its 50-day moving average.
- Persistently high oil prices and weak demand for spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which recorded $381 million in outflows Thursday, could limit a broader rally in risk assets.
Bitcoin  and gold (XAU) pared losses during Friday’s Asian hours alongside a recovery in stocks as the Japanese yen gave up early gains.
The largest cryptocurrency by market value recovered to nearly $82,000 after hitting lows below $81,000 overnight, according to CoinDesk data. At the time of writing, bitcoin was testing its 50-day simple moving average, a widely followed gauge of near-term market momentum. Other cryptocurrencies, such as ether , XRP (XRP), solana (SOL), and dogecoin  saw similar moves.
Crypto futures positions worth $435 million were liquidated over the past 24 hours, including $385 million in longs, a sign that leverage was skewed toward the bullish side.
Gold, a traditional haven asset, bounced back to $4,020 per ounce from an early low of $3,986, a level last seen on July 29.
Major Asian equity indices, including Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi, also rebounded from session lows. Nasdaq futures rose 0.17% to 29,190, up from 29,022 earlier in the day.
The risk-off tone had strengthened in early Asian trading as the yen climbed to 156.07 per U.S. dollar, its highest level since Sept. 18. Hotter-than-expected Japanese inflation data reinforced expectations of further Bank of Japan rate hikes, boosting the currency alongside a haven bid driven by AI-related jitters.
Yen moves often ripple through global markets because the currency has long been used to fund risk-on carry trades.
Those yen gains proved fleeting, however, with the currency quickly falling back toward 157 per U.S. dollar.
Whether the risk reset lasts may also depend on oil. WTI futures traded near $100, even after U.S. President Donald Trump invoked a Cold War-era law aimed at boosting fuel production. The move has yet to materially cool oil prices.
A sustained rise in oil could fuel global inflation and weigh on risk assets. Besides, a consistent demand for spot bitcoin ETFs is lacking for a steep price rally to materialize. On Thursday, these U.S.-listed funds lost $381 million in outflows, according to preliminary data from SoSoValue.

Bitcoin and gold prices recovered during Friday’s Asian trading session as the Japanese yen retreated and regional stock markets rebounded despite ongoing concerns regarding high global oil prices.

### Key Points
- Bitcoin recovered to nearly $82,000 after testing its 50-day moving average, while gold prices bounced back to $4,020 per ounce.

The volatility in these assets highlights how sensitive global markets remain to fluctuations in the Japanese yen and persistent energy costs. Investors are closely monitoring these trends to determine if the current recovery in risk assets can be sustained or if inflationary pressures will trigger further instability.

results.title: US tech stocks tumble as investors fret over AI spending
results.author: John Power
results.content:
US tech stocks have dropped sharply amid market jitters over the sustainability of companies’ enormous capital investments in AI.
The Nasdaq Composite, which is dominated by tech firms linked to the AI boom, fell 2.6 percent on Thursday, its steepest fall since the index tumbled 4.2 percent on June 5.
The broader S&P 500 slid 1.2 percent, the benchmark’s biggest drop since a 1.5 percent decline on July 29.
Apart from Apple, each of the “Magnificent 7”, which make up more than one-third of the overall market, saw substantial losses.
Meta dropped nearly 7 percent after it raised its projected capital spending for this year to $135bn to $145bn in its latest earnings report, even as the Facebook parent company’s net profit fell short of expectations.
Amazon fell 4.6 percent, while Nvidia dropped 4.4 percent.
Tesla and Alphabet both fell 3.1 percent, while Microsoft declined 2.2 percent.
Apple rose 1.2 percent.
The sell-off extended to other major tech players, including Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, both of which fell about 8 percent, and Broadcom, which slid 4.3 percent.
After the losses, the Nasdaq is about 5.8 percent off its all-time high, reached on October 6.
Rising oil prices since February, due to the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran, added to the downbeat mood.
Brent crude futures rose 4 percent on Thursday and continued to climb on Friday morning, taking the international benchmark above $114.20 a barrel, its highest since May.
Stocks slip in Asian trading
Major stock markets in Asia had a choppy session on Friday.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 fell more than 2 percent in morning trading before recouping some losses to close 0.3 percent lower.
South Korea’s KOSPI dropped as much as 3.5 percent before finishing up 0.3 percent.
The Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong gained 0.7 percent after earlier dropping about 0.5 percent.
Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, said the swings in the market appeared to be driven more by sentiment than underlying fundamentals.
“In short, nothing has changed. Investors have just decided to be afraid this week. Everyone I speak to points to a different cause for the downfall … It’s just a giant wall of worry,” Goldberg told Al Jazeera.
“There are legitimate concerns about the AI trade, but this level of shift in the markets is driven much more by investor sentiment than any tangible reason.”
US tech companies’ huge investments in AI have stoked intense debate about whether a market bubble is forming similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.
While some Wall Street analysts view current levels of investment in datacentres and graphics processing units as unsustainable, others argue that AI will revolutionise society to a degree that justifies the eye-watering sums involved.
Global AI investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.
results.summary:
US tech stocks experienced a sharp decline as investors grew increasingly concerned about the sustainability of massive capital investments in artificial intelligence and rising global oil prices.

### Key Points
- The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.6 percent on Thursday, marking its steepest single-day decline since June 5.
- Meta shares dropped nearly 7 percent after the company projected annual capital spending between $135 billion and $145 billion.
- Major tech firms including Amazon, Nvidia, Intel, and Advanced Micro Devices saw significant losses, while Apple shares rose 1.2 percent.
- Brent crude oil prices climbed above $114.20 per barrel, contributing to broader market instability and investor anxiety.
- Gartner forecasts global AI investment will reach $2.7 trillion by 2026 and $3.6 trillion by 2027.

### Why it Matters
The sell-off highlights growing market skepticism regarding whether the massive capital expenditures in AI infrastructure will yield sufficient long-term returns. This volatility reflects a broader debate among analysts over whether the current tech rally is a sustainable revolution or a speculative bubble similar to the dot-com era.

results.title: Happy 25th Anniversary, iPod
results.author: Hartley Charlton
results.content:
Apple today marks 25 years since the introduction of the original iPod, one of the company's most significant products and a major contributor to its expansion beyond the Mac.
Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPod on October 23, 2001, at a small press event in the Town Hall auditorium at Apple's Infinite Loop headquarters. Advertised as offering "1,000 songs in your pocket," the device combined a 5GB hard drive with a monochrome LCD display, a mechanical scroll wheel, and up to 10 hours of battery life.
The original model cost $399 and required a Mac with iTunes. Its FireWire connection transferred music and charged the battery, while automatic synchronization copied songs and playlists from the user's iTunes library. Apple said that an entire CD could be transferred in under 10 seconds and a collection of 1,000 songs in less than 10 minutes. The hard drive could also store documents and other files.
Ahead of the announcement, Apple invited the press to the unveiling of a "breakthrough digital device," specifying that it was not a Mac. Reports variously suggested a music player, a home stereo accessory, or a handheld device with handwriting recognition. MacRumors rumor roundup published two days before the event included the name "iPod."
The announcement received a mixed response. Our original coverage is still available, along with reader comments questioning the device's price, Mac-only compatibility, and significance. One reader described it as "far from revolutionary," while another wrote, "all this hype for something so ridiculous!"
The iPod went on sale on November 10, 2001, with readers reporting that they lined up to purchase it. Early forum discussions included complaints about fingerprints on the polished rear enclosure, charging temperatures, and sound quality, alongside a host of positive impressions from owners.
Hardware revisions followed in quick succession. The second-generation iPod adopted a touch-sensitive scroll wheel, while the third-generation model introduced the 30-pin Dock Connector in 2003. The full-size iPod gained a color display in 2004 and video playback in 2005.
The iPod mini was announced in January 2004, representing the first extension of the product line. It featured a smaller anodized aluminum enclosure in silver, gold, pink, blue, or green, and introduced the Click Wheel, which integrated playback buttons into the touch-sensitive scrolling surface. Apple adopted the same control for the fourth-generation full-size iPod later that year.
In 2005, Apple introduced both the iPod shuffle and iPod nano. The shuffle omitted a display and offered a smaller, simpler music player, while the nano replaced the mini with a thin design based on flash storage. Later iPod nano models added video playback, a video camera, and a touchscreen. The square sixth-generation model, introduced in 2010, could be worn on the wrist using third-party watch straps.
By April 2007, Apple had sold 100 million iPods, less than six years after the first model reached customers. By its 10th anniversary in 2011, sales had exceeded 304 million units.
The iPod touch arrived in September 2007, several months after the first iPhone went on sale. It featured a 3.5-inch Multi-Touch display, Wi-Fi, and Safari, without requiring a cellular plan.
Apple discontinued the iPod classic in September 2014, five years after its final hardware revision. The iPod nano and iPod shuffle followed in July 2017, leaving the iPod touch as the sole model.
The seventh-generation iPod touch received an A10 Fusion chip and up to 256GB of storage in May 2019. It remained on sale without further hardware updates until May 10, 2022, when Apple announced its discontinuation and said it would be available while supplies lasted.
In its announcement, Apple attributed the end of the lineup to the integration of music playback across its other products. Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, said that "the spirit of iPod lives on" through devices including the iPhone, Apple Watch, HomePod mini, Mac, iPad, and Apple TV.
results.summary:
Apple celebrates the 25th anniversary of the original iPod, the iconic portable music player that transformed the company and revolutionized the digital music industry starting in 2001.

### Key Points
- Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPod on October 23, 2001, featuring a 5GB hard drive and a mechanical scroll wheel for $399.
- The device promised "1,000 songs in your pocket" and utilized FireWire for rapid music synchronization with iTunes.
- Apple expanded the lineup over two decades to include the iPod mini, nano, shuffle, and the touchscreen-based iPod touch.
- By 2011, Apple had sold more than 304 million iPod units worldwide, cementing its status as a cultural phenomenon.
- Apple officially discontinued the final remaining model, the iPod touch, in May 2022, citing the integration of music features into other devices.

### Why it Matters
The iPod served as the primary catalyst for Apple's transition from a computer manufacturer into a dominant force in consumer electronics and digital media. Its success laid the essential groundwork for the iPhone and the modern ecosystem of integrated Apple services.

results.title: Capcom data breach exposes 11.7 million account records
results.author: Sinisa Markovic
results.content:
Capcom data breach exposes 11.7 million account records
Players who signed up for Capcom’s online account service may want to look twice at emails that seem to come from the company.
The company has disclosed that a third party gained unauthorized access to customer information linked to CAPCOM ID, the account people use to sign in to the company’s web services and to play some of its games online. It detected suspicious activity on October 19 and confirmed the intrusion the same day.
Capcom is the Japanese video game developer and publisher famous for Resident Evil, Street Fighter, Monster Hunter and Mega Man.
According to Capcom’s notice, the attackers got hold of 11,774,247 records worldwide containing email addresses along with system data about each account, including when it was created, the time of the last login, the number of logins, and the IP address used for the most recent sign-in.
For 43 of those records, the exposed data also included the account holder’s date of birth, gender, country or region, and nickname.
Capcom says it has found no evidence that passwords set by customers were compromised. The attackers did, however, change the passwords on 196 accounts without authorization, and the company has since reset them. Payment card information was not among the affected data, the company noted.
Email addresses registered with CAPCOM ID can still be used, the publisher said, though the stolen information could be used to send fraudulent messages posing as Capcom or related parties. Users who receive a suspicious email or message are asked to “refrain from accessing any URLs contained therein or opening any attached files.”
After spotting the activity, Capcom began blocking the access and worked to identify the method of attack.
On October 20 it set up an internal incident response headquarters and informed the Information Technology Security Oversight Committee, an external body that advises the company. A day later, it reported the incident to the Osaka Prefectural Police and to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.
The company says it has completed its emergency response and identified and addressed the attack method, without describing it, and that CAPCOM ID services and its games remain available.
Capcom plans to notify affected customers and has opened dedicated support channels by region, including a toll-free line in Japan and online inquiry forms for players in the Americas and in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
Its investigation is ongoing, and the company has said it will publish updates on its website if it finds further information that needs to be disclosed.
At the time of writing, no group has claimed responsibility for the attack.
This is not the first time Capcom has dealt with a cyberattack. In November 2020, the company suffered a ransomware attack that compromised the personal information of up to 350,000 customers, business partners and employees.
Capcom is not the only game company to report a cyberattack this year, with Rockstar Games, the developer of Grand Theft Auto and Red Dead Redemption, confirming an attack in April claimed by the ShinyHunters group.
results.summary:
Japanese video game developer Capcom confirmed a data breach involving unauthorized access to 11.7 million CAPCOM ID accounts, exposing email addresses and system login data for global users.

### Key Points
- Attackers accessed 11,774,247 records containing email addresses, account creation dates, and recent IP addresses.
- Personal details including gender, date of birth, and nicknames were exposed for 43 specific accounts.
- Capcom confirmed that no payment card information or customer passwords were compromised during the October 19 incident.
- Unauthorized parties successfully changed passwords for 196 accounts, which the company has since reset.
- The developer reported the breach to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.
- Capcom has established regional support channels and online inquiry forms to assist affected players worldwide.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the persistent cybersecurity risks facing major gaming publishers as they manage massive databases of user information. While financial data remained secure, the exposure of millions of email addresses increases the risk of targeted phishing campaigns against the company's player base.
